---
name: binding
description: "How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding: the safe boundary every binding keeps, and the routes binding-types and binding-symbols give types and symbols. Read before binding any item, and when reviewing bindings."
---

# Generating safe bindings

How a scheduled C item becomes a safe Rust binding.
A binding keeps the C implementation and puts a safe Rust API in front of it, shaped by the
item's analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes. A type takes the type
route, for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`binding-types`](types/SKILL.md)
describes; a symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, macros and
lifecycle strategies, as [`binding-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

## 1. Safe boundary

Any ABI or layout C still observes is preserved, and imported entities remain C-owned.

Rust consumers use safe APIs. Raw operations are confined to:

- wrapped-layout projection;
- wrapped FFI calls; and
- operations whose caller obligation cannot be represented in Rust types.

They sit in their module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)'
Unsafe regions section lays them out, and a region's soundness rests on the region alone:
each item it exposes is sound for every input the rest of its module can give it, the
invariants its unsafe code relies on being held in the region's own private fields or
guaranteed by the library the bindings hold C memory through or the standard library, never by data the native code can build or
change. It exposes no field its unsafe code relies on, and no `unsafe fn` beyond the
public ones whose obligation no type expresses.

The obligation of an `unsafe fn` that stores a value C keeps, such as a pointer a later
call follows, lasts as long as C holds it, in the object or in any copy C makes of it: until
a setter replaces it or a call clears it, the contract naming which, or else as long as its
holders live. It is never bounded by the calls that use the value, since safe code makes
those after the `unsafe` call has returned.

A confirmed C defect, a behaviour that departs from the C's specification as
[`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s `logic` objective orders it, is not
carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
Equivalence tests section describes.

A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
ports. Every unsafe block carries
the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.

An out-of-tree library's entity, such as libc's or libm's, is reached through the Rust
standard library wherever it provides it and the state the entity works on stays in Rust,
or crosses to C only as values the boundary converts: `errno` set from an `io::Error` by
an export gateway, a `struct stat` filled from an `fs::Metadata`. It is reached through the
library's bindings wherever that state is shared with C: a lock, a handle or an allocation
the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a
library's `decision` adopts or overrides; the first batch that needs the entity checks that
route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not
hold, and reports which in its final message, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section describes. An
entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.

name: binding-types
description: "How a scheduled C type becomes a safe Rust binding, binding's type route: its surface, safe layout, lifecycle and field accessors, unions as tagged enums, enums and typedefs. Read before binding any type, and when reviewing bindings."
---

# Binding types

How a scheduled C type becomes a safe Rust binding: the type route, which follows
[`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section; the symbols it reaches are
[`binding-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s. [`porting-types`](../../porting/types/SKILL.md)
starts from it.

## 1. Surface

A binding's surface is the fields and lifecycle primitives the public API publishes: in a
wrap batch that precedes its consumers, the fields those consumers access and the
type's lifecycle primitives, so that a type none of whose fields they access is bound
opaque.
Releasers, field disposers, cloners, constructors, casts and pointer-field semantics are
identified before a representation is chosen.

## 2. Safe layout

A type is bound as a safe layout over the raw type and its handles. The canonical wrapped
surface has three types, named as the conventions describe:

| type | role |
|---|---|
| `Foo` | layout-compatible newtype named in every owner and handle, and held by value only in Rust-owned storage (a local, or embedded) |
| `FooRef<'a>` | copyable shared borrowed handle with getters |
| `FooMut<'a>` | exclusive borrowed handle with setters, and shared and exclusive reborrows |

Its owners, which [Lifecycle](#3-lifecycle) describes, are named `FooBox` and `FooArc`, as
the conventions name them too. These names are what consumers use, whatever they name: here
pointer wrappers and owners over C's allocator, which a port changes, stage by stage, into
native borrows and owners, as [`porting-types`](../../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes,
without changing its consumers. A consumer relies only on what every form they may take
offers: their methods, their reborrows (`as_ref`, `as_mut`) and the dereferences the
native forms offer, which the pointer wrappers mirror. What one form offers beyond that,
such as an owner's raw access, is no part of the safe API.

No Rust reference to the wrapped C object is ever formed. Borrowed handles contain
pointers and carry lifetimes; references to handles cover Rust-owned handle storage only.
Layout access starts from `FooRef::as_ptr()` or `FooMut::as_mut_ptr()`, in small justified
unsafe blocks.

A synthetic type generator is bound as:

- a generic wrapper for a homogeneous family converging on the generator;
- an alias of a dominant concrete instance to the generator with its element wrapper; and
- specializations only for behaviour that differs from the generic surface.

## 3. Lifecycle

Every ownership variant the analysis supports has a representation.

Owners never dereference to `Foo`; they hand out handles. A sole owner, or a `Foo` value,
produces `FooRef` and `FooMut` through `as_ref()` and `as_mut()`. A shared owner without a
lock produces `FooRef` directly, and `FooMut` only when it can prove its reference is the
only one, or after copying the object. A shared owner whose object carries its own lock
produces both through read and write guards, which hold the lock while the handle lives.

Lifecycle and clone
strategies are stateless, layout-compatible and statically selected when the state is
recoverable from the object; runtime state is carried only when construction, destruction
or cloning needs external data.

A type's constructor and init routines are bound with its lifecycle policy, so that where
possible it is exported as a safe function returning the fully-formed object. Every type an
argument names is wrapped before it, since a wrap brings in its signature's types.

C lifecycle primitives are kept while C can allocate or free the storage.

A type whose address C keeps beyond the call that receives it, to read it, call back with it
or free it, as the analysis establishes, is never moved while C keeps it: a value of it
held by value is never handed to C to keep, and an owner that could move it out is
pinned.

Promoting construction-phase storage into an owner is unsafe, so it is encapsulated in the
type's safe constructor: consumers of the public API never call `assume_init` in their own
unsafe blocks.

Lifecycle routines are also scheduled as free symbols, although the type route emits them
as it binds their types; the symbol route, [`binding-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s,
skips those a type batch already emitted.

## 4. Field accessors

Each accessor follows from the ownership, mutability, nullability, cardinality and lifetime
findings, and every pointer-derived result is tied to the state that keeps it alive.

Getters that read `Foo`'s fields are methods in `impl FooRef` blocks taking `&self`, and
setters that write them are methods in `impl FooMut` blocks taking `&mut self`. A field is
read through the shared handle's pointer and written through the mutable handle's pointer,
projected with `addr_of!`, `addr_of_mut!`, `&raw const` or `&raw mut`, never with
`&(*p).field` or `&mut (*p).field`.

Each kind of field is expressed as follows:

- An owned-reference field has a replacement setter that drops the old owner, an owning
  getter that leaves the field valid, and a shared borrowed getter.
- A by-value wrapped field has a shared or mutable handle over the projected place.
- A stored borrow without an expressible lifetime has an unsafe setter whose caller
  contract carries the referent-lifetime obligation.
- Statically known owned and borrowed cases have distinct wrapper forms, with a shared
  trait where useful.
- A runtime ownership flag has separately checked owned and borrowed operations.
- A union field and its discriminator are one accessor of a tagged Rust enum, as
  [Unions](#5-unions) describes.
- Scalar and array variants have separate typed forms.
- A type-erased field takes a generic element type when it is known, and the discovered
  untyped lifetime strategy otherwise. One whose pointee's type a sibling field selects,
  as a kind tag does, is presented as a union is: one tagged enum over the tag and the
  pointer, each variant holding its type's safe form, read from both and written together,
  so that no setter writes the tag alone.
- `Send` and `Sync` are implemented only with a specific synchronization or immutability
  proof.

Translated dependent types and function pointers are used through their safe wrappers,
and strings, arrays and erased owners through real release strategies.

An inline function-pointer helper without an ownership-compatible wrapper gets one,
emitted with the type.

## 5. Unions

A union is not bound as a type of its own: the types its members hold are bound, and the
union is presented where it is used, a field accessor or a function's signature, as a
tagged Rust enum, with a variant for each member, each over its member's safe type. One
tagged enum stands in for the union at every use. Its tag is the discriminator the
analysis establishes as selecting the active member: a sibling field, a parameter, or a
predicate over sibling fields, such as a length that is zero only while an inline member
is active. Reading the union evaluates the discriminator to choose the variant, and
writing it writes both.

A union whose active member nothing beside it selects, its tag held by what refers to it,
such as the sign of the index that reaches it, is presented by an `unsafe` accessor for
each member, whose caller contract states which member must be active.

## 6. Enums

An enum is bound to a safe Rust type over the constants bindgen generates for it:

- a closed enum is a Rust enum, with a variant for each of its constants;
- an enum whose constants C combines as flags is a `#[repr(transparent)]` newtype over its
  integer type, with an associated constant for each of its constants and the bitwise
  operators, since a combination is no variant; and
- an enum without a name has no type to bind: its constants become constants of its
  integer type.

Beneath a closed enum's safe type sits its integer form, the interop layer C needs: a
`#[repr]` over the enum's integer type, as bindgen gives it, each constant's value its
variant's discriminant, and the conversions through which its values cross the boundary
as that integer. A value from C is converted fallibly where it enters Rust, since C may
pass one the enum does not name, which a Rust enum may not hold: such a value takes the
path the C gives an invalid value, or an error of the safe API where it gives none. A
binding keeps the integer form for good, since C implements what produces and consumes
the enum's values.

## 7. Typedefs

A typedef of its own, one that names no struct, union, enum or function pointer, gives
another name to a type that has a Rust form already: a primitive, an array, a pointer, or a
type another link unit or an out-of-tree library's wrapper owns. It is bound under its own
name to the Rust form the analysis shapes from its uses: an alias of the type it names where
they give it no meaning that type lacks, and a type of its own where they do, an invariant,
an ownership or a type erasure that an alias would flatten. Its raw form is no part of the
safe API, as [`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section describes, and it has no interop layer of
its own: its values cross the boundary as those of the type it names do.

carried into the safe API. Where Rust can tell the defect's input before the call, the
binding refuses it, with the error the C gives an invalid input; where it cannot, it
composes the item from the routines its C calls, through their own bindings and in the
C's order, correcting the defect, and its anchor is `Replaces`, as a port's is, its alias
kept. A lifecycle primitive that is defective only on a failure path is composed so,
while its policy still calls the primitives that are not. Each divergence is documented
on the item, and kept by a unit test, as [`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s
Equivalence tests section describes.

A dependency on a module that runs later, cut from a cycle, is reached through the safe
wrappers a wrap batch adds before its consumer, never through raw bindings. A wrapper over
the items of a module that will be ported is written as that module's API: the names,
ownership and error types its port keeps, so that its consumers do not change when it
ports. Every unsafe block carries
the safety comment [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section specifies.

the remaining C uses too. `dependencies.json` recommends a route for each entity, which a

route against the code it translates, takes another the decision allows where it does not
hold, and reports which in its final message, as

entity needed through a wrapper that lacks it is reported, never reached through raw
bindings.

# Binding types

How a scheduled C type becomes a safe Rust binding: the type route, which follows
[`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section; the symbols it reaches are
[`binding-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s. [`porting-types`](../../porting/types/SKILL.md)
starts from it.

## 1. Surface

A binding's surface is the fields and lifecycle primitives the public API publishes: in a
wrap batch that precedes its consumers, the fields those consumers access and the
type's lifecycle primitives, so that a type none of whose fields they access is bound
opaque.
Releasers, field disposers, cloners, constructors, casts and pointer-field semantics are
identified before a representation is chosen.

## 2. Safe layout

A type is bound as a safe layout over the raw type and its handles. The canonical wrapped
surface has three types, named as the conventions describe:

| type | role |
|---|---|
| `Foo` | layout-compatible newtype named in every owner and handle, and held by value only in Rust-owned storage (a local, or embedded) |
| `FooRef<'a>` | copyable shared borrowed handle with getters |
| `FooMut<'a>` | exclusive borrowed handle with setters, and shared and exclusive reborrows |

Its owners, which [Lifecycle](#3-lifecycle) describes, are named `FooBox` and `FooArc`, as
the conventions name them too. These names are what consumers use, whatever they name: here
pointer wrappers and owners over C's allocator, which a port changes, stage by stage, into
native borrows and owners, as [`porting-types`](../../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes,
without changing its consumers. A consumer relies only on what every form they may take
offers: their methods, their reborrows (`as_ref`, `as_mut`) and the dereferences the
native forms offer, which the pointer wrappers mirror. What one form offers beyond that,
such as an owner's raw access, is no part of the safe API.

No Rust reference to the wrapped C object is ever formed. Borrowed handles contain
pointers and carry lifetimes; references to handles cover Rust-owned handle storage only.
Layout access starts from `FooRef::as_ptr()` or `FooMut::as_mut_ptr()`, in small justified
unsafe blocks.

A synthetic type generator is bound as:

- a generic wrapper for a homogeneous family converging on the generator;
- an alias of a dominant concrete instance to the generator with its element wrapper; and
- specializations only for behaviour that differs from the generic surface.

## 3. Lifecycle

Every ownership variant the analysis supports has a representation.

Owners never dereference to `Foo`; they hand out handles. A sole owner, or a `Foo` value,
produces `FooRef` and `FooMut` through `as_ref()` and `as_mut()`. A shared owner without a
lock produces `FooRef` directly, and `FooMut` only when it can prove its reference is the
only one, or after copying the object. A shared owner whose object carries its own lock
produces both through read and write guards, which hold the lock while the handle lives.

Lifecycle and clone
strategies are stateless, layout-compatible and statically selected when the state is
recoverable from the object; runtime state is carried only when construction, destruction
or cloning needs external data.

A type's constructor and init routines are bound with its lifecycle policy, so that where
possible it is exported as a safe function returning the fully-formed object. Every type an
argument names is wrapped before it, since a wrap brings in its signature's types.

C lifecycle primitives are kept while C can allocate or free the storage.

A type whose address C keeps beyond the call that receives it, to read it, call back with it
or free it, as the analysis establishes, is never moved while C keeps it: a value of it
held by value is never handed to C to keep, and an owner that could move it out is
pinned.

Promoting construction-phase storage into an owner is unsafe, so it is encapsulated in the
type's safe constructor: consumers of the public API never call `assume_init` in their own
unsafe blocks.

Lifecycle routines are also scheduled as free symbols, although the type route emits them
as it binds their types; the symbol route, [`binding-symbols`](../symbols/SKILL.md)'s,
skips those a type batch already emitted.

## 4. Field accessors

Each accessor follows from the ownership, mutability, nullability, cardinality and lifetime
findings, and every pointer-derived result is tied to the state that keeps it alive.

Getters that read `Foo`'s fields are methods in `impl FooRef` blocks taking `&self`, and
setters that write them are methods in `impl FooMut` blocks taking `&mut self`. A field is
read through the shared handle's pointer and written through the mutable handle's pointer,
projected with `addr_of!`, `addr_of_mut!`, `&raw const` or `&raw mut`, never with
`&(*p).field` or `&mut (*p).field`.

Each kind of field is expressed as follows:

- An owned-reference field has a replacement setter that drops the old owner, an owning
  getter that leaves the field valid, and a shared borrowed getter.
- A by-value wrapped field has a shared or mutable handle over the projected place.
- A stored borrow without an expressible lifetime has an unsafe setter whose caller
  contract carries the referent-lifetime obligation.
- Statically known owned and borrowed cases have distinct wrapper forms, with a shared
  trait where useful.
- A runtime ownership flag has separately checked owned and borrowed operations.
- A union field and its discriminator are one accessor of a tagged Rust enum, as
  [Unions](#5-unions) describes.
- Scalar and array variants have separate typed forms.
- A type-erased field takes a generic element type when it is known, and the discovered
  untyped lifetime strategy otherwise. One whose pointee's type a sibling field selects,
  as a kind tag does, is presented as a union is: one tagged enum over the tag and the
  pointer, each variant holding its type's safe form, read from both and written together,
  so that no setter writes the tag alone.
- `Send` and `Sync` are implemented only with a specific synchronization or immutability
  proof.

Translated dependent types and function pointers are used through their safe wrappers,
and strings, arrays and erased owners through real release strategies.

An inline function-pointer helper without an ownership-compatible wrapper gets one,
emitted with the type.

## 5. Unions

A union is not bound as a type of its own: the types its members hold are bound, and the
union is presented where it is used, a field accessor or a function's signature, as a
tagged Rust enum, with a variant for each member, each over its member's safe type. One
tagged enum stands in for the union at every use. Its tag is the discriminator the
analysis establishes as selecting the active member: a sibling field, a parameter, or a
predicate over sibling fields, such as a length that is zero only while an inline member
is active. Reading the union evaluates the discriminator to choose the variant, and
writing it writes both.

A union whose active member nothing beside it selects, its tag held by what refers to it,
such as the sign of the index that reaches it, is presented by an `unsafe` accessor for
each member, whose caller contract states which member must be active.

## 6. Enums

An enum is bound to a safe Rust type over the constants bindgen generates for it:

- a closed enum is a Rust enum, with a variant for each of its constants;
- an enum whose constants C combines as flags is a `#[repr(transparent)]` newtype over its
  integer type, with an associated constant for each of its constants and the bitwise
  operators, since a combination is no variant; and
- an enum without a name has no type to bind: its constants become constants of its
  integer type.

Beneath a closed enum's safe type sits its integer form, the interop layer C needs: a
`#[repr]` over the enum's integer type, as bindgen gives it, each constant's value its
variant's discriminant, and the conversions through which its values cross the boundary
as that integer. A value from C is converted fallibly where it enters Rust, since C may
pass one the enum does not name, which a Rust enum may not hold: such a value takes the
path the C gives an invalid value, or an error of the safe API where it gives none. A
binding keeps the integer form for good, since C implements what produces and consumes
the enum's values.

## 7. Typedefs

A typedef of its own, one that names no struct, union, enum or function pointer, gives
another name to a type that has a Rust form already: a primitive, an array, a pointer, or a
type another link unit or an out-of-tree library's wrapper owns. It is bound under its own
name to the Rust form the analysis shapes from its uses: an alias of the type it names where
they give it no meaning that type lacks, and a type of its own where they do, an invariant,
an ownership or a type erasure that an alias would flatten. Its raw form is no part of the
safe API, as [`binding`](../SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section describes, and it has no interop layer of
its own: its values cross the boundary as those of the type it names do.

Read before writing any wrapper, owner, lifecycle strategy, callable type or export, when judging a crate for adoption, and when testing or reviewing one." --- # ffibox ffibox is the library a campaign's Rust expresses C's ownership and lifetime conventions through, in both directions: memory C allocates, frees, copies, refcounts or locks, held from Rust behind a safe API, and memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Its primitives stand in for raw pointers and hand-written `Drop` impls wherever C aliases a value; what C does not alias is plain Rust. Its `README.md` is read in full before the first wrapper is written, and each section below names the documents under its `docs/` that its stage reads, also in full. Which primitive serves which C declaration, and how each is built, is those documents'. A representation ffibox cannot express is hand-written, as its `docs/hand-written.md` describes, with the same seam and safety-comment discipline. Its goals and non-goals, `docs/goals.md`, are what a change to ffibox is judged against, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes. What follows is how ffibox serves each stage: each section names the skill and section it adds to, and states only what ffibox adds there. ## Planning ### Dependencies › Adopted crates A candidate crate's soundness is read against the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists, each of which ffibox excludes from the campaign's own bindings: the crate qualifies where its safe API excludes them too, by whatever means it uses. ## Binding workflow ### Binding workflow › Rust tree The workspace depends on ffibox by path, on the checkout the host provides, which is on the campaign's working branch of it, `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }` in Crustify's image, so that each run records its revision among its task's `revisions`. The path is the checkout's canonical one, with no symbolic link on it, and a `[patch]` that redirects another source of ffibox names the same: compile-fail snapshots normalize a path dependency only where the compiler's paths match the dependency's canonical directory. ## Binding and porting Binding reads `docs/ownership.md`, `docs/borrows.md`, `docs/patterns.md`, `docs/vtables.md` and `docs/hand-written.md`; porting reads `docs/outbound.md` too. ### Binding types A type that stays interoperable with C is bound through ffibox's primitives wherever they apply, as `docs/ownership.md` and `docs/borrows.md` walk from its C declaration to them. ### Binding types › Safe layout While a type keeps its C layout, `define_ctype!` mints `Foo`, `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its owners are aliases of ffibox's owners over the policy that names its lifecycle routines: `pub type FooBox = CBox;`, and `CArc` for `FooArc`. A value held inline that disposes its resources on drop is a `CVal`. ### Binding symbols › Functions A C routine's status convention becomes a `Result` through `status`, an object returned through an out-parameter a return value through `from_c_out` or `from_raw_out`, and C's iteration conventions iterators, as `docs/patterns.md` maps them. ### Binding symbols › Function pointers A function pointer's callable type is a `CCallback`, where C holds it for a call or a borrow, or a `CCallbackBox`, where C keeps it until it releases its context. Its Rust half is a closure, a `CClosure` or a `CPayload`, which C reaches through its trampoline; its C half is a C function with its context, a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, which Rust calls, built only inside the crate through its `unsafe` constructor. A trampoline is the panic barrier, `callback::barrier`, which also guards an export's body. A struct of function pointers a library calls into, implemented by a Rust trait, is a `CTable` whose slots `impl_cvtable!` mints, over the binding's own `unsafe impl CVtable`, as `docs/vtables.md` describes; a table C implements is held as any other C object. A family of hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table. ### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C. ### Porting › FFI boundary An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does with the Rust it reaches: - the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`, `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return its owners and handles; - memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C frees it through an exported release; - a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a `CPayload`; and - the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`. ### Porting types › Structs Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as [Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its `port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then the Rust ones. A `port/memory` before its `port/layout` keeps them ffibox's and changes their policy to `RustAlloc` alone: `FooBox` becomes `CBox`, its handles unchanged, until its `port/layout` makes it `Box`, or `Pin>` while C keeps its address. Between a struct's `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, its layout is native while C still allocates or frees its storage, and ffibox's single-object owners, which hold only C-layout types, cannot hold it. Where C releases it with its allocation family's free alone, and the native type is not zero-sized and needs no drop (`size_of::() != 0` and `!core::mem::needs_drop::()`, both asserted at compile time), and C does not keep its address, `FooBox` is `Box>` and a counted run of them `Vec>`, `P` the family's `Copy` policy with the alignment the family guarantees: an existing `CLenAlloc` policy of the family, or one declared with `impl_clenalloc!`'s `align =`. A box is built with `CAllocator::try_box`, which refuses an over-aligned type at compile time and returns C's out-of-memory failure, and handed to C with `Box::into_raw_with_allocator`; a run grows with `Vec::try_reserve`, keeping C's out-of-memory failure, and is handed to C through `CVec::try_from` and `into_raw_parts`. A pointer C hands back is adopted with `Box::from_raw_in`, under the conditions `CBox::into_box`'s documentation lists, and a run with `Vec::from_raw_parts_in`, its length as its capacity, under the allocator's fit rule. Its `port/memory` makes them `Box` and `Vec`. ## Testing ### Testing › UB tests The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test. ## Reviewing Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`. ### Reviewing › Objectives A workset's use of ffibox's primitives is reviewed against ffibox's documentation, and its hand-written representations against the contract ffibox would have enforced. Under `ub`, the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists are the checklist: each is excluded by the primitive or the producer's contract it names, or is a finding. ### Reviewing-reports › Reports A soundness or ergonomics gap in ffibox itself, in its safe primitives or its unsafe FFI seams, is a defect in a tool: a proposal, as any tool defect is. --- name: soundness description: "The patterns by which safe Rust over C has reached undefined behaviour in Crustify's campaigns, each with what prevents it and which check catches it, and how the catalogue grows from proven findings. Read before analysing, binding or porting any item, before writing its UB tests, and when reviewing for UB or contracts." --- # Soundness patterns The ways a binding or a port of C has let safe Rust reach undefined behaviour, or met a memory-safety defect of the C that it had to keep out of its safe API. Every pattern here has a proven finding of a campaign behind it: the catalogue records what went wrong, not what could. An item's analysis asks of each pattern whether the item can meet it, and a review for UB or contracts reads the item against the same list, so that a defect one module met is not met again in the next. ## 1. Patterns Each pattern has an id, which a finding's report names. What prevents a pattern is stated as what the Rust does; [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md) and [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) give the routes that do it. ### 1.1 Values the C trusts | id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by | |---|---|---|---| | `unchecked-arithmetic` | The C computes with a value a safe caller controls and does not check it: a signed overflow, a shift, a size that wraps with its header, a zero divisor. | The Rust checks the value's range before the call, sizes past `isize::MAX` included, and refuses what the C would compute wrongly. | UBSan, review | | `diverging-precheck` | A check in Rust repeats the C's parsing or evaluation and differs from what the C then computes. | The Rust validates the exact value the C will use, or computes the result itself and hands the C only that. | UBSan | | `degenerate-input` | The C reads out of bounds on an input its own validation accepts, such as an empty string beside others or a null pointer for a string. | Every wrapper that can route the input to that reader refuses or normalises it, the indirect routes included. | ASan | | `variant-mismatch` | A tagged, variable-size value of another variant than its container expects is passed on, and the C sizes its buffers by the container's. | The Rust compares the value's variant with the container's before any call that looks it up or formats it. | ASan | ### 1.2 Memory and ownership | id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by | |---|---|---|---| | `size-known-to-c` | Only the C knows an object's true size or layout: an opaque type, a pointer a tag types, a base struct its callbacks read past, an array sized by a count. Rust builds it too small or types it wrongly. | Such an object is allocated through the C alone, a tagged pointer is typed only where its tag is vouched for, and an object whose callbacks read more than Rust built is refused. | ASan, review | | `hidden-dependency` | A handle, a lent pointer or a callback outlives something it depends on without showing it: a parent it points back to, a global the program may close, lent memory the C copied into a second slot. | The handle's lifetime is tied to that owner, or it keeps the owner alive; a pointer the C stores is bounded by its longest-lived reader. | ASan, Miri, review | | `failure-leaves-state` | A failure path of the C, most often a failed allocation, leaves an object uninitialised, freed, wrongly sized or half written and still returns, sometimes reporting success. | The Rust trusts nothing the C leaves after a failure: it validates outputs again, does not reuse the object, and composes the operation itself where the C's error path is unsafe. | ASan, UBSan, review | | `allocator-rule` | The binding vouches for a rule of alignment or allocation that some build or allocator of the C does not keep: the maximum alignment, a zero-size resize, who may free whose storage. | It vouches only for what every configured allocator guarantees, and checks alignment at each constructor that copies. | Miri, UBSan, review | | `adoption-condition` | An adoption takes ownership without stating when the C owns the storage: a sentinel pointer at zero capacity, one element listed twice, a buffer a pool still tracks. | The contract states the exact condition, and the Rust checks it before the owner can free or resize. | ASan, review | | `count-wrap` | A reference count the C does not check wraps once safe Rust can leak clones, and the object is freed early. | A count that can wrap within a process's lifetime is checked before each increment, and the clone fails or aborts before it wraps. | Miri, review | | `uninitialised-as-data` | Memory the C leaves unwritten is exposed as initialised Rust data, or the argument that the C writes it is false on some path. | The Rust views it as uninitialised until every path of the C is shown to write it; an export takes raw pointers and builds no reference over memory its caller may have left unwritten. | Miri, review | | `aliasing-at-the-boundary` | A pointer the C keeps is derived from a borrow that a later reborrow ends, or Rust holds a reference over memory the C still writes or shares. | Every pointer the C keeps is derived from the original raw pointer, and a reference is handed out only over a span no C writer or co-owner reaches. | Miri, BSan, review | ### 1.3 Threads and callbacks | id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by | |---|---|---|---| | `unsynchronised-global` | The C reads and writes global state, or initialises it lazily on first use, without synchronisation, so that safe calls on unrelated objects race. | The Rust initialises or serialises that state before any safe call reaches it. | TSan, review | | `assumed-locking` | A `Send` or `Sync` proof assumes the C object's own locking covers every access, but a path skips the lock, reads after releasing it, or the object has none. | Thread safety is derived from every reader and writer of each field. | review | | `callback-state` | A trampoline mishandles a panic, a refusal or a re-entry: a stored panic goes stale or a nested call drops it, a drop panics, the C goes on after a refusal, or the callback runs under a lock of the C. | A stored panic or stop belongs to one outermost call of the C, no drop panics, and a stop is promised only where the C can be stopped. | review | A `# Safety` contract or a `// SAFETY:` proof that is wrong in a way no pattern above names is still a finding: a contract is derived again from every safe method that relies on it whenever one is added. ## 2. Findings A finding of the `ub` or `contracts` objective names its pattern, or `new`, as [`reviewing-reports`](../../verification/reviewing/reports/SKILL.md)'s Reports section describes. A sanitizer's false positive is no finding and names none. A finding of a known pattern means that its statement did not let the analysis recognise the case, or that what prevents it was not enough. A finding that is `new` is a pattern the catalogue lacks. ## 3. Evolution The catalogue changes only from findings a reproducer proves, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes: - a `new` finding is proposed as a pattern once it is stated without the target's names, with the finding as its evidence; one that can only be stated in the target's names is that campaign's lesson; - a pattern whose findings recur has its statement or its prevention sharpened, from the findings that escaped it; and - a pattern no campaign has met since it was written stays: its absence is what the catalogue is for. What tells whether the catalogue works is the count of findings of known patterns, over the modules integrated since a pattern was written, taken together: it falls against the modules before, or the catalogue is not what prevents them. One module alone tells nothing, since modules differ. The unsafe sites the reviews read, which the count would be taken against, are not recorded yet. The count of `new` findings tells how much of what goes wrong the catalogue does not hold yet. A family of hooks that carries no context is trampolines over `callback::barrier`, not a table. ### Binding symbols › Lifecycle strategies Each lifecycle is held by the owner `docs/ownership.md` chooses for its shape, over the policy that names its routines; a policy with state, such as an allocator context, is held by `CBoxState`. A Rust value whose release C drives, such as a refcounted user payload, is a `CPayload`, released through the routine it gives C. ### Porting › FFI boundary An export gateway is built from the primitives `docs/outbound.md` chooses for what C does with the Rust it reaches: - the lifecycle routines C still calls on a ported type are `export_cnew!`, `export_cdrop!` and `export_cdupclone!` over the type's policy, which take and return its owners and handles; - memory C frees comes from the allocator C frees it with: Rust's, `RustAlloc`, when C frees it through an exported release; - a callback C passes an export is a `CFn` or a `CFnBox`, and a value C keeps a `CPayload`; and - the gateway's body runs in `callback::barrier`. ### Porting types › Structs Until a ported struct's `port/layout`, its handles are ffibox's, as [Binding types › Safe layout](#binding-types--safe-layout) describes; from it on, `FooRef` and `FooMut` are aliases of native borrows. Its owners stay ffibox's until its `port/memory`, or until its `port/layout` where that comes first, as below, their policy calling its lifecycle routines, C's through their raw bindings until each is ported, then the Rust ones. A `port/memory` before its `port/layout` keeps them ffibox's and changes their policy to `RustAlloc` alone: `FooBox` becomes `CBox`, its handles unchanged, until its `port/layout` makes it `Box`, or `Pin>` while C keeps its address. Between a struct's `port/layout` and its `port/memory`, its layout is native while C still allocates or frees its storage, and ffibox's single-object owners, which hold only C-layout types, cannot hold it. Where C releases it with its allocation family's free alone, and the native type is not zero-sized and needs no drop (`size_of::() != 0` and `!core::mem::needs_drop::()`, both asserted at compile time), and C does not keep its address, `FooBox` is `Box>` and a counted run of them `Vec>`, `P` the family's `Copy` policy with the alignment the family guarantees: an existing `CLenAlloc` policy of the family, or one declared with `impl_clenalloc!`'s `align =`. A box is built with `CAllocator::try_box`, which refuses an over-aligned type at compile time and returns C's out-of-memory failure, and handed to C with `Box::into_raw_with_allocator`; a run grows with `Vec::try_reserve`, keeping C's out-of-memory failure, and is handed to C through `CVec::try_from` and `into_raw_parts`. A pointer C hands back is adopted with `Box::from_raw_in`, under the conditions `CBox::into_box`'s documentation lists, and a run with `Vec::from_raw_parts_in`, its length as its capacity, under the allocator's fit rule. Its `port/memory` makes them `Box` and `Vec`. ## Testing ### Testing › UB tests The public seam interface ffibox exports on a type is meant to be exercised inside the crate only, as an escape hatch for external consumers, so it gets no UB tests: a test of it, for UB or functionality, is a unit test. ## Reviewing Reviewing reads `docs/goals.md`. ### Reviewing › Objectives A workset's use of ffibox's primitives is reviewed against ffibox's documentation, and its hand-written representations against the contract ffibox would have enforced. Under `ub`, the hazards `docs/goals.md`'s G9 lists are the checklist: each is excluded by the primitive or the producer's contract it names, or is a finding. ### Reviewing-reports › Reports A soundness or ergonomics gap in ffibox itself, in its safe primitives or its unsafe FFI seams, is a defect in a tool: a proposal, as any tool defect is. --- name: soundness description: "The patterns by which safe Rust over C has reached undefined behaviour in Crustify's campaigns, each with what prevents it and which check catches it, and how the catalogue grows from proven findings. Read before analysing, binding or porting any item, before writing its UB tests, and when reviewing for UB or contracts." --- # Soundness patterns The ways a binding or a port of C has let safe Rust reach undefined behaviour, or met a memory-safety defect of the C that it had to keep out of its safe API. Every pattern here has a proven finding of a campaign behind it: the catalogue records what went wrong, not what could. An item's analysis asks of each pattern whether the item can meet it, and a review for UB or contracts reads the item against the same list, so that a defect one module met is not met again in the next. ## 1. Patterns Each pattern has an id, which a finding's report names. What prevents a pattern is stated as what the Rust does; [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md) and [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) give the routes that do it. ### 1.1 Values the C trusts | id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by | |---|---|---|---| | `unchecked-arithmetic` | The C computes with a value a safe caller controls and does not check it: a signed overflow, a shift, a size that wraps with its header, a zero divisor. | The Rust checks the value's range before the call, sizes past `isize::MAX` included, and refuses what the C would compute wrongly. | UBSan, review | | `diverging-precheck` | A check in Rust repeats the C's parsing or evaluation and differs from what the C then computes. | The Rust validates the exact value the C will use, or computes the result itself and hands the C only that. | UBSan | | `degenerate-input` | The C reads out of bounds on an input its own validation accepts, such as an empty string beside others or a null pointer for a string. | Every wrapper that can route the input to that reader refuses or normalises it, the indirect routes included. | ASan | | `variant-mismatch` | A tagged, variable-size value of another variant than its container expects is passed on, and the C sizes its buffers by the container's. | The Rust compares the value's variant with the container's before any call that looks it up or formats it. | ASan | ### 1.2 Memory and ownership | id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by | |---|---|---|---| | `size-known-to-c` | Only the C knows an object's true size or layout: an opaque type, a pointer a tag types, a base struct its callbacks read past, an array sized by a count. Rust builds it too small or types it wrongly. | Such an object is allocated through the C alone, a tagged pointer is typed only where its tag is vouched for, and an object whose callbacks read more than Rust built is refused. | ASan, review | | `hidden-dependency` | A handle, a lent pointer or a callback outlives something it depends on without showing it: a parent it points back to, a global the program may close, lent memory the C copied into a second slot. | The handle's lifetime is tied to that owner, or it keeps the owner alive; a pointer the C stores is bounded by its longest-lived reader. | ASan, Miri, review | | `failure-leaves-state` | A failure path of the C, most often a failed allocation, leaves an object uninitialised, freed, wrongly sized or half written and still returns, sometimes reporting success. | The Rust trusts nothing the C leaves after a failure: it validates outputs again, does not reuse the object, and composes the operation itself where the C's error path is unsafe. | ASan, UBSan, review | | `allocator-rule` | The binding vouches for a rule of alignment or allocation that some build or allocator of the C does not keep: the maximum alignment, a zero-size resize, who may free whose storage. | It vouches only for what every configured allocator guarantees, and checks alignment at each constructor that copies. | Miri, UBSan, review | | `adoption-condition` | An adoption takes ownership without stating when the C owns the storage: a sentinel pointer at zero capacity, one element listed twice, a buffer a pool still tracks. | The contract states the exact condition, and the Rust checks it before the owner can free or resize. | ASan, review | | `count-wrap` | A reference count the C does not check wraps once safe Rust can leak clones, and the object is freed early. | A count that can wrap within a process's lifetime is checked before each increment, and the clone fails or aborts before it wraps. | Miri, review | | `uninitialised-as-data` | Memory the C leaves unwritten is exposed as initialised Rust data, or the argument that the C writes it is false on some path. | The Rust views it as uninitialised until every path of the C is shown to write it; an export takes raw pointers and builds no reference over memory its caller may have left unwritten. | Miri, review | | `aliasing-at-the-boundary` | A pointer the C keeps is derived from a borrow that a later reborrow ends, or Rust holds a reference over memory the C still writes or shares. | Every pointer the C keeps is derived from the original raw pointer, and a reference is handed out only over a span no C writer or co-owner reaches. | Miri, BSan, review | ### 1.3 Threads and callbacks | id | pattern | what prevents it | caught by | |---|---|---|---| | `unsynchronised-global` | The C reads and writes global state, or initialises it lazily on first use, without synchronisation, so that safe calls on unrelated objects race. | The Rust initialises or serialises that state before any safe call reaches it. | TSan, review | | `assumed-locking` | A `Send` or `Sync` proof assumes the C object's own locking covers every access, but a path skips the lock, reads after releasing it, or the object has none. | Thread safety is derived from every reader and writer of each field. | review | | `callback-state` | A trampoline mishandles a panic, a refusal or a re-entry: a stored panic goes stale or a nested call drops it, a drop panics, the C goes on after a refusal, or the callback runs under a lock of the C. | A stored panic or stop belongs to one outermost call of the C, no drop panics, and a stop is promised only where the C can be stopped. | review | A `# Safety` contract or a `// SAFETY:` proof that is wrong in a way no pattern above names is still a finding: a contract is derived again from every safe method that relies on it whenever one is added. ## 2. Findings A finding of the `ub` or `contracts` objective names its pattern, or `new`, as [`reviewing-reports`](../../verification/reviewing/reports/SKILL.md)'s Reports section describes. A sanitizer's false positive is no finding and names none. A finding of a known pattern means that its statement did not let the analysis recognise the case, or that what prevents it was not enough. A finding that is `new` is a pattern the catalogue lacks. ## 3. Evolution The catalogue changes only from findings a reproducer proves, as [`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md) describes: - a `new` finding is proposed as a pattern once it is stated without the target's names, with the finding as its evidence; one that can only be stated in the target's names is that campaign's lesson; - a pattern whose findings recur has its statement or its prevention sharpened, from the findings that escaped it; and - a pattern no campaign has met since it was written stays: its absence is what the catalogue is for. What tells whether the catalogue works is the count of findings of known patterns, over the modules integrated since a pattern was written, taken together: it falls against the modules before, or the catalogue is not what prevents them. One module alone tells nothing, since modules differ. The unsafe sites the reviews read, which the count would be taken against, are not recorded yet. The count of `new` findings tells how much of what goes wrong the catalogue does not hold yet.

content.content:
# ffibox

Generic smart pointers and traits for building safe Rust wrappers over C
types and pointers, in both directions: memory C owns, held from Rust, and
memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Designed for arbitrary
user-space C interop, including the case where you need direct field access
and a C-ABI-compatible layout (porting C internals to Rust in place), not just
opaque-handle wrapping.

## Why

Wrapping a C API in Rust means re-homing C's ownership and lifecycle
conventions into RAII. The recurring shapes:

- A C-allocated object with a destructor (`free`), and maybe a copy (`dup`).
- A constructor or allocator (`foo_alloc`, `malloc`, `calloc`) whose result
  must be released by its paired free.
- A refcounted object shared by several holders (`up_ref` / `unref`), maybe
  with a C lock over the state they mutate.
- Types with multiple or runtime-conditional destructors.
- A by-value struct whose teardown disposes its fields but not the struct.
- An owned length-aware buffer or NUL-terminated `char *` with a C destructor.
- A type-erased `void *` that stays opaque end to end.

Each shape gets one owner type, generic over a **policy** — a type you declare
that names the C routines. `impl_cdrop!` and its siblings bind a C routine to a
policy; a type alias names the pair: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`.

## Mental model in one paragraph

No reference to C-owned memory is formed while anything may write or free it:
objects are reached through handles, and only a run of bytes nothing writes
while it is lent is a `&CStr` or `&[u8]`. Each C type gets a layout type
`Foo` (`#[repr(transparent)]` over `ffi::foo`; `Foo<'r>` when the C object
borrows its parent) and two borrowed handles, `FooRef<'a>` / `FooMut<'a>`,
each one pointer wide and carrying the getters and setters; field access projects a raw pointer out of the handle. Ownership
comes in three shapes: `CBox<Foo, P>` is the sole owner of an object behind a
pointer and releases it through the policy `P`; `CArc<Foo, P>` is one of
several counted references and hands out the shared handle, the exclusive one
only when the count proves it sole, and — for an object with a C lock — a
`CGuard` whose `FooLocked<'a>` handle reaches the state that lock protects; and
`CVal<Foo, P>` holds the object inline and disposes its resources on drop.
A policy that also constructs gives `CBox` and `CArc` safe constructors that
allocate through it, so a safely built owner is always freed by the routine
paired with its allocator.
Strings, buffers and borrowed runs get their own types; a buffer drops its
elements, so a `foo **` of owned objects releases each one.

The other direction uses the same terms. `RustAlloc` is the policy over Rust's
allocator, so an object Rust allocates is held as one C allocated, and
`CAllocator` is a C allocation family as the standard `Allocator`, so a
`Box` or `Vec` holds memory C frees; `CClosure`
and `CPayload` put a Rust closure behind a C function pointer and its
context, for one call or until C releases it; `CFn` and `CFnBox` hold a C
function and its context that Rust calls, and `CCallback` and `CCallbackBox`
either half; `CTable` holds Rust state behind a C table of function
pointers C calls into, its slots minted by `impl_cvtable!` from a trait the
Rust side implements; the `export_*!` macros offer a policy to C as the
routine it calls, with the owner and handle types in its signature.
[docs/ownership.md](docs/ownership.md) lists the owners and the policies;
[docs/borrows.md](docs/borrows.md) lists the handles. Each walks from a C
declaration to the type it wants.

## Install

```toml
[dependencies]
ffibox = "0.1"
```

ffibox needs Rust 1.100 or later (`rust-version` in `Cargo.toml`), the first
release with the standard `Allocator` interface, which `CAllocator` implements
over a C allocation family.

ffibox is `#![no_std]`. The `std` feature (on by default) selects
`std::process::abort` for the unrecoverable-failure path (`Clone` or
`make_mut` when the C copy or up_ref fails), where without it that path is a
double-panic, and lets `CClosure`, `CTable`'s slots and `callback::barrier`
catch a panic before it reaches C. The `alloc` feature, which `std` enables,
adds `RustAlloc`, `CPayload`, `CCallbackBox` and `CTable`, which allocate
through Rust's global allocator, and the conversions between ffibox's owners
and `Box` / `Vec`; nothing else allocates but through a policy the consumer
chose, as `CAllocator` allocates through its family.

```toml
[dependencies]
ffibox = { version = "0.1", default-features = false }
```

## Documentation

Every wrapper answers one question first: **does dropping the Rust value
release the object?** This is about who *releases* the object, not who
allocated it — a `CBox` usually points at memory C allocated.

- **Yes** — it is owned → [docs/ownership.md](docs/ownership.md)
- **No** — C, or a parent object, releases it → [docs/borrows.md](docs/borrows.md)

When it is Rust's memory that C holds, calls or reads →
[docs/outbound.md](docs/outbound.md).

| doc | what is in it |
|-----|---------------|
| [goals.md](docs/goals.md) | what the primitives aim for, in both directions, and how each aim is checked |
| [examples.md](docs/examples.md) | eight self-contained wrappers, each compiled as a doctest |
| [ownership.md](docs/ownership.md) | `CBox`, `CBoxState`, `CVal`, `CStrBox`, `CVec`, `CArc`; the lifecycle policies; picking an owner and a policy; `Box` and `Vec` over a C allocator (`CAllocator`) |
| [borrows.md](docs/borrows.md) | `Foo`, `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooLocked`, `CGuard`, `CGuardedRef`, `CSlice`, `CSliceMut`, `CNullTerminated`; where the accessors live; the seam traits |
| [outbound.md](docs/outbound.md) | Rust's side: `RustAlloc`, the callbacks (`CClosure`, `CPayload`, `CFn`, `CFnBox`, `CCallback`, `CCallbackBox`), C tables (`CTable`), out-parameters, the panic barrier, the `export_*!` macros |
| [vtables.md](docs/vtables.md) | C tables of function pointers implemented in Rust: `CTable`, `impl_cvtable!`, their receivers, re-entry, panics and release, and the design |
| [patterns.md](docs/patterns.md) | C's iteration, error and callback conventions as Rust's iterators, `Result` and closures |
| [hand-written.md](docs/hand-written.md) | the wrappers `define_ctype!` cannot express (a layout type generic over a type), and the owners no policy expresses |

Upgrading? [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) says what each release changes, and
how to migrate code that still compiles but behaves differently.

or conditions.


## Acknowledgements

This material is based upon work supported by the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency (DARPA)
Translating All C To Rust (TRACTOR) program under Agreement No. HR00112590134.
# Borrows

A borrow is a handle over an object something else releases — C, or a parent
object. It is one pointer wide, carries a lifetime, and is never a Rust
reference to the C object itself.

For the owning side — values whose drop releases the object — see
[ownership.md](ownership.md).

## The handles

| Scope | Type | From | Role |
|-------|------|------|------|
| per C type | `Foo` | `define_ctype!` | the layout, the C struct's size: `#[repr(transparent)]` over `ffi::foo`, embeds by value in a `#[repr(C)]` mirror, and is what a `CBox` points at. Never referenced over C-owned memory. Also the value itself when it owns no resources (a rational `{ num, den }`). |
| | `FooRef<'a>` | `define_ctype!` | shared borrow, one pointer wide, `Copy`; the getters |
| | `FooMut<'a>` | `define_ctype!` | exclusive borrow, move-only; the setters, and the getters through `as_ref()` |
| per C lock | `FooLocked<'a>` | `impl_cguarded!` | exclusive borrow under the C lock, move-only; getters and setters for the state the lock protects, the unlocked getters through `as_ref()` |
| lock | `CGuard<'a, Foo>` | ffibox | a held C lock, unlocking on drop — `MutexGuard`; `as_locked()` → `FooLocked<'_>`, `as_ref()` → `FooRef<'_>` |
| guarded borrow | `CGuardedRef<'a, Foo>` | ffibox | an object under one lock covering all of it (`CGuardedAll`), never released — typically a C global (`'static`); only `lock()`, whose `as_locked()` is `FooMut` — `&Mutex<_>` |
| views | `CSlice<'a, T>` / `CSliceMut<'a, T>` | ffibox | any borrowed run of elements — a buffer's, a struct field's, a getter's — as handles or copies, never a `&[T]`; only a run of plain values nothing writes while it is lent is a `&[T]` instead, as [Choosing a borrow](#choosing-a-borrow) describes |
| | `CNullTerminated<'a, T>` | ffibox | a NULL-terminated array of pointers (`char **`, `foo **`), iterated as `&CStr`s or `FooRef`s |

A layout type that carries a lifetime, over a C object that keeps a pointer
to its parent, is `define_ctype!`'s too: `define_ctype!(Blob<'r>, BlobRef,
BlobMut, ffi::blob, phantom = &'r Repo)` gives `Blob<'r>`, `BlobRef<'a, 'r>`
and `BlobMut<'a, 'r>`, the marker deciding how `Blob` varies in `'r`. A
wrapper that needs type parameters (derived sub-types over a generic field) is
written by hand against the same contract — see
[Under the hood](hand-written.md). Its policies still come from the macros
where they take the type.

## Conventions

- **Accessors live on the handles.** Getters on `FooRef<'a>` taking `&self`,
  setters on `FooMut<'a>` taking `&mut self`; `FooMut` reaches the getters with
  `as_ref()`, so they are written once. Both project a raw pointer out of the
  handle and read or write through `addr_of!` / `addr_of_mut!`.
- **Every holder reaches the handles the same way:** `as_ref()` / `as_mut()` on
  `Foo`, `CBox`, `CBoxState`, `CVal` and `FooMut` itself (where `as_mut()` is
  the reborrow `&mut` gets implicitly: `helper(m.as_mut())` keeps `m`);
  `as_ref()` on `CArc`, whose exclusive handle comes only from `get_mut()` /
  `make_mut()`; `as_ref()` / `as_locked()` on a `CGuard` and on `FooLocked` (where
  `as_locked()` reborrows). `CSliceMut` reborrows the same
  way, and splits and sub-ranges like `&mut [T]`. Never `Deref`:
  `Deref::Target` cannot name a lifetime taken from `&self`, and since `FooRef`
  is `Copy`, a `Deref<Target = FooRef<'a>>` on `FooMut` would let safe code copy
  a shared handle out while keeping the exclusive one.
- **No reference covers C memory anything may write.** `&FooRef` covers one pointer of Rust stack,
  never the object. The one place a reference covers a C struct's bytes is
  `Foo::as_ref` / `as_mut` on a value Rust holds inline. A run of bytes an

  describes; otherwise it is a `CSlice`.

  `FooRef` (`from_ptr`, `as_ptr` and the `void *` pair), `CMutSeam` on `FooMut`
  (`from_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr` and the `void *` pair) and `CLockedSeam` on
  `FooLocked` (`as_mut_ptr` alone). Import them wherever the seam is used, in

  handles. Their methods are provided once, by ffibox, so the wrapper crate
  defines no raw-pointer method of its own for them. The inbound half is also

  that the pointee is a valid `Foo`, the borrows its lifetimes name included,

## Choosing a borrow

Reached when dropping the Rust value does *not* release the object. When it
does, the answer is an owner — see
[ownership.md](ownership.md#choosing-an-owner-what-shape-is-the-owned-thing).

- **No — C, or a parent object, releases it.** Borrow it:
  - one object → `FooRef<'a>` / `FooMut<'a>`, its lifetime tied to whatever
    keeps it alive (a parent's handle, the call);
  - a run of elements → `CSlice<'a, T>` / `CSliceMut<'a, T>`;
  - a counted run of immutable bytes an object lends, `const uint8_t *data`
    with its `size_t len` (from a getter pair, or two fields) → `&'a [u8]`
    from `core::slice::from_raw_parts`, tied to the shared handle's `'a`, as a
    NUL string is a `&CStr`. A run of other `CPlainElem` values is the same
    `&'a [T]`. The SAFETY comment shows, from C's contract, that:
    - nothing writes, moves or frees the bytes while the shared handle lives:
      no routine reachable through a `FooRef` writes, grows or reallocates
      them (not one on `FooRef`, not one on a `FooLocked` taken beside it, not
      another thread's, if `Foo` is `Sync`); a write reachable only through
      `FooMut` is excluded by the borrow;

      lifetime covers, not by the next call that refills a shared buffer; and
    - `data` addresses `len` initialised bytes in one allocation. A NULL or
      empty run returns `&[]` without the call, since `from_raw_parts` takes
      no NULL even for a length of 0.

    reallocates behind a `const` pointer, or state another thread writes, the
    run is a `CSlice<'a, u8>` built with `CSlice::from_raw_parts`, which forms
    no reference: `elems`, `copy_to_slice` and `to_cvec` copy the bytes out.
    The element type does not decide between the two, since a `u8` is plain
    either way: who may write the bytes does. A caller that keeps the bytes
    past the object's borrow takes an owned copy;

    `Iterator` of the elements' borrows; a `count` + `get(i)` pair or a
    `->next` chain is `(0..n).map(get)` or `iter::successors` over the safe
    getter;

    typically a C global and the C lock protecting it → `CGuardedRef<'a, Foo>`,
    `'static` for a global, with `impl_cguarded!(Foo, all, …)`;
  - a NUL string → `&CStr` / `&str` / `&[u8]` tied to the owner's borrow,

  sent to a thread) cannot be expressed as a lifetime; copy the child into an

Only a wrapper `define_ctype!` cannot express — a layout type generic over a
type — needs this layer, and so does an owner no policy expresses:

lifetimes is not hand-written: `define_ctype!` declares it,
`define_ctype!(Blob<'r>, BlobRef, BlobMut, ffi::blob, phantom = &'r Repo)`,
as [examples.md](examples.md#a-layout-type-with-a-lifetime--define_ctype-with-phantom)
shows. One already written by hand is the same layout, and moves to the macro
when its module is next touched, or stays.

A C table a library calls into and Rust implements (a backend, a stream:
a struct of function pointers, each passed the table) is not hand-written
either: `CTable` lays it out with its state, recovers the state in each slot,
guards re-entry, puts each slot behind the panic barrier and releases it once,
and `impl_cvtable!` mints the slots, as [vtables.md](vtables.md) describes.

`unsafe extern "C" fn` whose body is `CTable::enter`, in a hand-written
`CSlots<S>` impl beside an `unsafe impl CVtable<S>`.

their seams, against the items below. Its policies are not, unless no macro
takes them:

  a `define_ctype!` one does: `impl_cdrop!(BlobFree, Blob<'_>, ffi::blob_free)`

  `impl_cguarded!` name the lifetime, `<'r> BlobFree, Blob<'r>`, as
  [ownership.md](ownership.md#policies--what-teardown-means) explains.
- **A routine of another shape** (a slot, an out-parameter, extra arguments)
  is no reason to hand-write a policy: a private `unsafe fn` adapter passed to

A `CVec` releases an array of owners element by element, then frees the

# ffibox

Generic smart pointers and traits for building safe Rust wrappers over C
types and pointers, in both directions: memory C owns, held from Rust, and
memory Rust owns that C holds, calls or reads. Designed for arbitrary
user-space C interop, including the case where you need direct field access
and a C-ABI-compatible layout (porting C internals to Rust in place), not just
opaque-handle wrapping.

## Why

Wrapping a C API in Rust means re-homing C's ownership and lifecycle
conventions into RAII. The recurring shapes:

- A C-allocated object with a destructor (`free`), and maybe a copy (`dup`).
- A constructor or allocator (`foo_alloc`, `malloc`, `calloc`) whose result
  must be released by its paired free.
- A refcounted object shared by several holders (`up_ref` / `unref`), maybe
  with a C lock over the state they mutate.
- Types with multiple or runtime-conditional destructors.
- A by-value struct whose teardown disposes its fields but not the struct.
- An owned length-aware buffer or NUL-terminated `char *` with a C destructor.
- A type-erased `void *` that stays opaque end to end.

Each shape gets one owner type, generic over a **policy** — a type you declare
that names the C routines. `impl_cdrop!` and its siblings bind a C routine to a
policy; a type alias names the pair: `pub type FooBox = CBox<Foo, FooFree>;`.

## Mental model in one paragraph

No reference to C-owned memory is formed while anything may write or free it:
objects are reached through handles, and only a run of bytes nothing writes
while it is lent is a `&CStr` or `&[u8]`. Each C type gets a layout type
`Foo` (`#[repr(transparent)]` over `ffi::foo`; `Foo<'r>` when the C object
borrows its parent) and two borrowed handles, `FooRef<'a>` / `FooMut<'a>`,
each one pointer wide and carrying the getters and setters; field access projects a raw pointer out of the handle. Ownership
comes in three shapes: `CBox<Foo, P>` is the sole owner of an object behind a
pointer and releases it through the policy `P`; `CArc<Foo, P>` is one of
several counted references and hands out the shared handle, the exclusive one
only when the count proves it sole, and — for an object with a C lock — a
`CGuard` whose `FooLocked<'a>` handle reaches the state that lock protects; and
`CVal<Foo, P>` holds the object inline and disposes its resources on drop.
A policy that also constructs gives `CBox` and `CArc` safe constructors that
allocate through it, so a safely built owner is always freed by the routine
paired with its allocator.
Strings, buffers and borrowed runs get their own types; a buffer drops its
elements, so a `foo **` of owned objects releases each one.

The other direction uses the same terms. `RustAlloc` is the policy over Rust's
allocator, so an object Rust allocates is held as one C allocated, and
`CAllocator` is a C allocation family as the standard `Allocator`, so a
`Box` or `Vec` holds memory C frees; `CClosure`
and `CPayload` put a Rust closure behind a C function pointer and its
context, for one call or until C releases it; `CFn` and `CFnBox` hold a C
function and its context that Rust calls, and `CCallback` and `CCallbackBox`
either half; `CTable` holds Rust state behind a C table of function
pointers C calls into, its slots minted by `impl_cvtable!` from a trait the
Rust side implements; the `export_*!` macros offer a policy to C as the
routine it calls, with the owner and handle types in its signature.
[docs/ownership.md](docs/ownership.md) lists the owners and the policies;
[docs/borrows.md](docs/borrows.md) lists the handles. Each walks from a C
declaration to the type it wants.

## Install

```toml
[dependencies]
ffibox = "0.1"
```

ffibox needs Rust 1.100 or later (`rust-version` in `Cargo.toml`), the first
release with the standard `Allocator` interface, which `CAllocator` implements
over a C allocation family.

ffibox is `#![no_std]`. The `std` feature (on by default) selects
`std::process::abort` for the unrecoverable-failure path (`Clone` or
`make_mut` when the C copy or up_ref fails), where without it that path is a
double-panic, and lets `CClosure`, `CTable`'s slots and `callback::barrier`
catch a panic before it reaches C. The `alloc` feature, which `std` enables,
adds `RustAlloc`, `CPayload`, `CCallbackBox` and `CTable`, which allocate
through Rust's global allocator, and the conversions between ffibox's owners
and `Box` / `Vec`; nothing else allocates but through a policy the consumer
chose, as `CAllocator` allocates through its family.

```toml
[dependencies]
ffibox = { version = "0.1", default-features = false }
```

## Documentation

Every wrapper answers one question first: **does dropping the Rust value
release the object?** This is about who *releases* the object, not who
allocated it — a `CBox` usually points at memory C allocated.

- **Yes** — it is owned → [docs/ownership.md](docs/ownership.md)
- **No** — C, or a parent object, releases it → [docs/borrows.md](docs/borrows.md)

When it is Rust's memory that C holds, calls or reads →
[docs/outbound.md](docs/outbound.md).

| doc | what is in it |
|-----|---------------|
| [goals.md](docs/goals.md) | what the primitives aim for, in both directions, and how each aim is checked |
| [examples.md](docs/examples.md) | eight self-contained wrappers, each compiled as a doctest |
| [ownership.md](docs/ownership.md) | `CBox`, `CBoxState`, `CVal`, `CStrBox`, `CVec`, `CArc`; the lifecycle policies; picking an owner and a policy; `Box` and `Vec` over a C allocator (`CAllocator`) |
| [borrows.md](docs/borrows.md) | `Foo`, `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooLocked`, `CGuard`, `CGuardedRef`, `CSlice`, `CSliceMut`, `CNullTerminated`; where the accessors live; the seam traits |
| [outbound.md](docs/outbound.md) | Rust's side: `RustAlloc`, the callbacks (`CClosure`, `CPayload`, `CFn`, `CFnBox`, `CCallback`, `CCallbackBox`), C tables (`CTable`), out-parameters, the panic barrier, the `export_*!` macros |
| [vtables.md](docs/vtables.md) | C tables of function pointers implemented in Rust: `CTable`, `impl_cvtable!`, their receivers, re-entry, panics and release, and the design |
| [patterns.md](docs/patterns.md) | C's iteration, error and callback conventions as Rust's iterators, `Result` and closures |
| [hand-written.md](docs/hand-written.md) | the wrappers `define_ctype!` cannot express (a layout type generic over a type), and the owners no policy expresses |

Upgrading? [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) says what each release changes, and
how to migrate code that still compiles but behaves differently.

# Borrows

A borrow is a handle over an object something else releases — C, or a parent
object. It is one pointer wide, carries a lifetime, and is never a Rust
reference to the C object itself.

For the owning side — values whose drop releases the object — see
[ownership.md](ownership.md).

## The handles

| Scope | Type | From | Role |
|-------|------|------|------|
| per C type | `Foo` | `define_ctype!` | the layout, the C struct's size: `#[repr(transparent)]` over `ffi::foo`, embeds by value in a `#[repr(C)]` mirror, and is what a `CBox` points at. Never referenced over C-owned memory. Also the value itself when it owns no resources (a rational `{ num, den }`). |
| | `FooRef<'a>` | `define_ctype!` | shared borrow, one pointer wide, `Copy`; the getters |
| | `FooMut<'a>` | `define_ctype!` | exclusive borrow, move-only; the setters, and the getters through `as_ref()` |
| per C lock | `FooLocked<'a>` | `impl_cguarded!` | exclusive borrow under the C lock, move-only; getters and setters for the state the lock protects, the unlocked getters through `as_ref()` |
| lock | `CGuard<'a, Foo>` | ffibox | a held C lock, unlocking on drop — `MutexGuard`; `as_locked()` → `FooLocked<'_>`, `as_ref()` → `FooRef<'_>` |
| guarded borrow | `CGuardedRef<'a, Foo>` | ffibox | an object under one lock covering all of it (`CGuardedAll`), never released — typically a C global (`'static`); only `lock()`, whose `as_locked()` is `FooMut` — `&Mutex<_>` |
