  - an out-parameter slot → `&'a mut MaybeUninit<T>` from
    `ptr.cast::<MaybeUninit<T>>().as_mut()`; no ffibox type;
  - a `void *` → if it is really a `ffi::foo`, erase a `FooRef` with
    `as_void_ptr` and recover it with `from_void_ptr` (generically,
    `T::ref_from_void_ptr` / `T::mut_from_void_ptr` for `T: CCell`); if it is a
    cookie never looked inside, pass the raw `*mut c_void` through unchanged.

  A borrow that must outlive its parent's scope (stored next to the parent,
  sent to a thread) cannot be expressed as a lifetime; copy the child into an
  owned object instead.
# Hand-written wrappers

Only a wrapper `define_ctype!` cannot express — a layout type generic over a
type — needs this layer, and so does an owner no policy expresses:
[an array freed by one routine](#an-array-freed-by-one-routine) that does
more than free its elements and itself. A layout type that carries only
lifetimes is not hand-written: `define_ctype!` declares it,
`define_ctype!(Blob<'r>, BlobRef, BlobMut, ffi::blob, phantom = &'r Repo)`,
as [examples.md](examples.md#a-layout-type-with-a-lifetime--define_ctype-with-phantom)
shows. One already written by hand is the same layout, and moves to the macro
when its module is next touched, or stays.

A C table a library calls into and Rust implements (a backend, a stream:
a struct of function pointers, each passed the table) is not hand-written
either: `CTable` lays it out with its state, recovers the state in each slot,
guards re-entry, puts each slot behind the panic barrier and releases it once,
and `impl_cvtable!` mints the slots, as [vtables.md](vtables.md) describes.
Only a slot the macro cannot express is written by hand, as an
`unsafe extern "C" fn` whose body is `CTable::enter`, in a hand-written
`CSlots<S>` impl beside an `unsafe impl CVtable<S>`.

What is hand-written for such a wrapper is the layout type, its handles and
their seams, against the items below. Its policies are not, unless no macro
takes them:

- **A layout type generic over a type** (`Stack<T, S>`) has no elided form,
  so each of its policies is an `unsafe impl<T, S>` by hand.
- **A hand-written layout type with a lifetime** takes every policy macro, as
  a `define_ctype!` one does: `impl_cdrop!(BlobFree, Blob<'_>, ffi::blob_free)`
  implements `CDrop<Blob<'r>>` for every `'r`, and `impl_cdupclone!` and
  `impl_cguarded!` name the lifetime, `<'r> BlobFree, Blob<'r>`, as
  [ownership.md](ownership.md#policies--what-teardown-means) explains.
- **A routine of another shape** (a slot, an out-parameter, extra arguments)
  is no reason to hand-write a policy: a private `unsafe fn` adapter passed to
  the macro gives it the shape the macro calls, as
  [ownership.md](ownership.md#policies--what-teardown-means) describes.

| Item | Role | Source |
|------|------|--------|
| `CCell` | the linking trait: `type C` (the FFI type), `type Ref<'a>`, `type Mut<'a>`, and the provided, `unsafe` inbound seam (`ref_from_ptr`, `mut_from_ptr` and their `void *` twins). Its `unsafe impl` promises that `Self` is layout-compatible with `C`, and that `Ref` / `Mut` are `#[repr(transparent)]` over `CBorrowedPtr<'a, Self>` with no `Drop`, and `Mut` invariant in `Self` (a `PhantomData<&'a mut Self>` field) — ffibox builds handles from that layout, and checks their size at compile time. | `src/traits.rs` |
| `CRefSeam` / `CMutSeam` / `CLockedSeam` | the handles' seams, every method provided from the layout `CCell` (or `CGuarded`) guarantees: implement them on hand-written handles with `type Cell = Foo;`, as the macros do, or the handles have no `as_ptr` / `as_mut_ptr`. | `src/traits.rs` |
| `CBorrowedPtr<'a, T>` | what every handle wraps: one pointer tagged with the borrow's lifetime, `Copy` and covariant like `&'a T`. | `src/refs.rs` |
| `CPlainElem` | marker for plain-data elements: every bit pattern is a valid value and there is no C-side identity. It admits `&[T]` from a `CVec`, as a `CSliceElem` (a wrapped C type implements `CCell` instead, so `&[Foo]` does not typecheck), and makes copies read out of memory C keeps writing sound. Not the same as initialized: an unfilled buffer is `CVec<MaybeUninit<T>, _>` until `assume_init`. | `src/traits.rs` |
| `CSliceElem` | elements a `CVec` hands out as `&[T]` / `&mut [T]`: every `CPlainElem`, and the owners — `CBox`, `CArc` and `CStrBox`, bare or in an `Option`, and `CVal` — whose references cover a Rust value, never C memory. A hand-written owner implements it on the same terms. | `src/traits.rs` |

**Layout.** `CBox`, `CArc` and `CStrBox` are `#[repr(transparent)]` over their
pointer, and their policy is stateless, held in no bytes: `Option<CBox<Foo, P>>`
is a `ffi::foo *`, NULL for `None`, as Rust guarantees for `Option<NonNull<_>>`.
So it takes a raw pointer's place in a `#[repr(C)]` struct, a `foo **` buffer
and an `extern "C"` signature alike. A policy with state fails to build in
them; it is held by `CBoxState<Foo, P>`, `#[repr(C)]` over `{ptr, policy}`,
which crosses as a raw pointer. `CVal<Foo, P>` is the size of `Foo` under a
stateless policy; a buffer is pointer + length, the pointer NULL when empty,
as C's `{ T *ptr; size_t len; }`.

## An array freed by one routine

A `CVec` releases an array of owners element by element, then frees the
buffer through `CLenDrop`, which frees the buffer only (see
[ownership.md](ownership.md#choosing-an-owner-what-shape-is-the-owned-thing)).
That covers a C routine whose body is only those frees. One that does more
— takes a lock, updates a count, or releases an element other than by
freeing it — is not a policy: the wrapper writes the owner itself, as `CVec`
is written:

- private fields, the pointer and the length, adopted by an `unsafe`
  constructor whose contract is the routine's: the array is one the routine
  frees, and its non-null elements are distinct allocations it owns;
- a `Drop` that calls the routine once, with both;
- the elements handed out as borrows tied to `&self` — `FooRef<'_>` through
  `CRefSeam::from_ptr`, `&CStr`, a `CSlice` of the pointers, which copies
  them out — never as `&mut` to a slot, through which safe code would store
  a pointer, or NULL, that the routine then frees.

name: testing-builds
description: "The builds tests run against and how coverage is measured: the prebuilt variants, private builds, coverage instrumentation, objects, suites and figures, and a worklist's coverage. Read before building or choosing a test build, and before measuring or comparing coverage."
---

# Testing builds

The builds every test of [`testing`](../SKILL.md) runs against, and how coverage is measured
over them.

## 1. Builds

Tests run against the target's prebuilt, immutable builds, recorded as the `variants` of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`: each an out-of-tree `dir` and the `configure` and `build`
commands run from it, its `version` raised whenever a command changes. They are:

- `plain`, the functional baseline;
- `coverage`, the coverage-instrumented build for campaign measurements, instrumented as
  [Coverage](#2-coverage) describes; and
- one variant per sanitizer the campaign enables, whose tests build the Rust with the same
  LLVM sanitizer as the C, the C's clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version as for
  coverage, so that one runtime serves both and a report from the Rust's own unsafe code is
  caught too, and whose C consumers that link the safe crate's Rust static library, from a
  module's switch on, link one built with the same instrumentation:
  - `asan-ubsan`, the general build, which FFI and lifecycle tests use;
  - `msan`, which instruments every component, the standard library included;
  - `tsan`, separate from `asan-ubsan`, since ASan and TSan instrument the same memory
    operations and their runtimes conflict; and
  - `bsan`, when BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain is installed and answers its version;
    it instruments the C through its own matched clang.

A Rust- or bindgen-only change reuses a matching variant: same C revision, `build.json`
version, compiler and instrumentation. Nothing writes into a variant's `dir`: each run's
logs and outputs go to paths of its own. A change to the compiled target, or no matching
variant, needs a private build, which the raw bindings link when `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` names
it in place of a variant, and the shared variants are rebuilt once that change lands.

## 2. Coverage

Coverage is counted with one instrument for C and Rust, so that a C figure and a Rust
figure, and the campaign's figures and those of a crate it is compared with, are counted
alike, and count the code under test only:

- **Instrumentation.** The `coverage` variant compiles the C with clang's source-based
  coverage, `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping` in its compile and link flags,
  from a clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version, and the Rust is compiled on that
  nightly with `-C instrument-coverage`. One profiling runtime counts both, into a profile
  per process and module (`LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<dir>/%p-%m.profraw`), and the nightly's
  `llvm-profdata` and `llvm-cov` read both. gcc's coverage instrumentation and gcov are not used: their
  lines follow the line table of the optimized code, which the optimization level changes,
  so their figures cannot be compared with Rust's.
- **Test code.** Test code is not instrumented, so it is neither credited as covered nor
  counted as code to cover. Counted, it would inflate the suite that runs it, whose own
  lines run whenever it does, and deflate every other suite, whose denominator would hold
  lines it never runs. Every test item of the measured crate, under `#[test]`,
  `#[cfg(test)]` or a `cfg` that requires `test`, carries `#[coverage(off)]`, which covers
  everything nested in it, and the crate root enables `#![feature(coverage_attribute)]`.
  The attributes are added in a scratch copy of the measured tree under `crustify/tmp/`,
  which is measured in its place, so that the measured crates are not changed. Integration
  test crates, examples, benches, the crate root's build script and the generated raw
  bindings under `sys/` are left out of the report by path. Test code that is not an item, such as a `#[cfg(test)]`
  block inside a library function, stays instrumented, and is reported with the figures.
- **Objects.** C coverage is read from the objects the tests load: the variant's shared
  libraries, or the object files a crate links statically, every TU compiled into them
  counting, and one no test reaches at zero. A figure covers the sources of the library it
  names, selected by directory, so that the copies of its inline functions and of its TUs
  that other libraries compile, the configuration headers the build generates and the C's
  own tests count toward none. Rust coverage is read from every test and doctest binary of
  the crate. All objects are passed for every suite, so that every suite has the same
  denominator.
- **Suites.** Each suite runs alone, into its own profile directory, merged into one
  profile; the total merges the suites' profiles, so it is their union, never their sum.
  Doctests are a suite of their own.
- **Figures.** The figures are the totals `llvm-cov report` prints, unmodified: line,
  function and region coverage, line coverage leading. Its per-line views (`llvm-cov show`
  and the LCOV export) count lines differently, marking the bodies of C macro definitions
  as executed: they locate gaps, and never compute a figure.
- **Comparisons.** A crate the campaign is compared with is measured the same way: its
  test items marked in a scratch copy, its own release of the C built as the `coverage`
  variant is, its suites run alone, and its figures read from `llvm-cov report`. A
  comparison names its scope, and both sides are measured over the same one.

### 2.1 A worklist's coverage

A worklist's tests run against the campaign's `coverage` variant, measured as
above, and coverage is inspected for the C and Rust execution
paths belonging to the worklist. Focused tests are added to cover its reachable uncovered
paths. Paths that remain uncovered because they are unreachable, environment-dependent, or
intentionally nondeterministic are reported as such.

Coverage is maximized, not gated. Each worklist reports its regions and branches beside
its lines, and which of its types' states and transitions, as the analysis lists them, its
tests reach. In a port, a module's C is the reference until its switch: its coverage
under the module's equivalence tests shows how much of its behaviour they compare, set
against what its own C tests reach. From the switch on, the module's coverage is its
Rust's.
---
name: conventions
description: "Naming, tree layout, anchors and test placement of the Rust a campaign generates. Read before writing, homing or reviewing generated Rust or tests."
---

# Crustify coding conventions

These are the shared, mechanical contracts of the code a campaign generates: how it is
named, where it sits, how it records what it translated and where its tests go. The
toolchain, edition, lints and formatting it is held to are [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Naming

The workspace's lints enforce the standard Rust casing below, as [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s
Lints section describes.

The safe surface uses ordinary Rust naming: `snake_case` for functions, methods and
modules, `UpperCamelCase` for types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and
statics. A C name's library or owning-type prefix is dropped wherever the crate, module or
receiver already supplies it, and the idiomatic Rust term is preferred over a
transliterated C one. The filled anchor records the C name, so renaming costs no
traceability. Names that cross the language boundary keep their C-derived spelling, as
below.

### 1.1 Functions

A C function's raw binding is `sys::<name>`. Its safe wrapper is a free function homed in
the owning module, named by the rules above. When one C function has several valid
ownership contracts, each safe variant has a distinct, descriptive name.

### 1.2 Types

A wrapped C type is the layout-compatible newtype `Foo`, named by the rules above; its
shared and exclusive borrowed handles are `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its sole and
counted owners `FooBox` and `FooArc`. A port keeps these names while what they name
changes, as [`porting-types`](../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes. A typedef that
names a type under another name, which its item lists among its `typedefs`, is a
`pub type` alias of the type's Rust form.

A function pointer a typedef declares is named after its typedef. One written inline is
named after the site that declares it, its holder's name followed by its own and `Fn`: a
field's `<Struct><Field>Fn`, a parameter's `<Function><Param>Fn`, a return's
`<Function>ReturnFn` and a global's `<Global>Fn`.

### 1.3 Shims

A callable macro shim is `crustify_<NAME>`.

### 1.4 Exports

Each ported module has one raw ABI gateway, its `ffi_export` region, as
[Unsafe regions](#21-unsafe-regions) describes, whose exports use `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` under the bare C names: the
module's functions and globals that C outside the module references, another module's TU
or a C test or executable that stays, the `static inline` functions its headers define
included. The exports serve that C, which reaches the module through them once it has
switched. A function or global only the module's own C references is not exported: that
C leaves the build with the module at its switch, and its callers are Rust from then
on; nor are static functions and static globals, which nothing outside their TU reaches.
The target's public C API, for C outside the target, is deferred: exports serve the
target's own remaining C alone, and that API is a layer of its own over the native Rust API,
added once the modules it covers are ported.
<!-- TODO: that layer, a C-compatible ABI over the ported public API, is not specified
yet. Until it is, a C consumer outside the target does not survive a port. -->
An export is removed, with the raw binding that reaches it, by its symbol's `port/unexport`,
after the switch that removes the last C that calls it, takes its address or
accesses it. A C test tied to the module that stays, using only its public API, does not
hold an export back: it checks the export while other C needs it, and leaves with it.

### 1.5 Export features

Each module's `ffi_export` is compiled only under the safe crate's Cargo feature
`ffi-export-<tu>`, with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root, every character
that is not an ASCII letter or digit replaced by `-`. The feature is off until the module
switches, so that its exports never collide with the C they replace, and the switch
deletes it, its gateway compiling unconditionally from then on.

## 2. Crates, modules, and TUs

The Rust tree is the repository's own, as [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Tree section lays it
out, all relative to the repository's root:

- `Cargo.toml` - the safe crate's manifest, which also declares the workspace.
- `src/lib.rs` - the safe crate's root, with one `cfg`-gated module per link unit.
- `src/<link-unit>/` - one sub-dir per link unit.
- `src/sys.rs` and `sys/<link-unit>/` - the raw bindings, one public module per link unit,
  laid out as [`bindgen`](../bindgen/SKILL.md) describes.

The safe crate is named after its repository, `<repo>-crustify`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section names it:
a name crates.io leaves free, which tells it apart from the source's own Rust bindings,
such as `git2` for libgit2.

Within a link unit's sub-dir, the tree follows the module decomposition in `modules.json`
exactly, and preserves the C layout as far as the idiomatic organization of a Rust tree
allows:

- each module is one `.rs` file, at its translation unit's path below the C root with the
  `.rs` extension: its TU and the headers bundled with it have no files of their own,
  since Rust has no headers;
- a header module is one `<stem>_h.rs` file, at its header's path;
- the two modules of a split foundational TU share the TU's file;
- C directories become Rust modules: a directory's `.rs` file sits beside the directory,
  as `<dir>.rs` and `<dir>/`, and declares the modules within it, or is the module of a TU
  with the directory's name where there is one; `mod.rs` files are not used; and
- a file or directory name that is not a Rust identifier is sanitized, hyphens to
  underscores, and a Rust keyword takes a trailing underscore.

Where a C layout has no idiomatic Rust counterpart, the tree adapts it in the conventional
Rust way and keeps the C path recognizable. A batch names the `.rs` file each of its items
belongs in, as `src/<link-unit>/…/<file>.rs`. Entities sharing a
definition site co-home. A home may be shared across waves.

### 2.1 Unsafe regions

A module's unsafe code is confined to at most two inline child modules of its file, its
unsafe regions, so that the rest of the file, its native code, holds none:

- `mod ffi_import`: what the module reaches in C: its calls through the raw bindings, the C
  layouts it wraps with their handles and accessors, the owners and lifecycle policies over
  C's allocator, and the trampolines and contexts through which C calls a Rust closure
  back; and
- `mod ffi_export { use super::*; … }`: the gateway through which C reaches the module by
  symbol, as [Exports](#14-exports) describes, compiled only under its
  [export feature](#15-export-features).

Unsafe code is every `unsafe` block, `unsafe fn`, `unsafe impl`, `unsafe extern` block and
`#[unsafe(…)]` attribute, and every invocation of another crate's macro that expands to
one, such as one that mints a type over a C layout, which the compiler's `unsafe_code` lint does not
see. Outside the regions, only the raw bindings hold any. The regions take the lint back as
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section describes.

A region exposes to its module only what [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section lets it expose, and the module re-exports the public items a region defines, as
`pub use ffi_import::{Foo, FooBox, FooMut, FooRef};`, so that their paths do not depend on
which side defines them. A type's inherent `impl` blocks may be split between the native
code and a region: each method is visible as its own visibility says, counted from the
module that holds its block, so that a region's private helpers stay hidden from the
native code.

A region exists only while it holds something. A wrap's items are in `ffi_import`. A port
writes its item in the native code, and keeps in the regions only the C form the item
keeps, as [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) describes; a wrapped item it ports leaves
`ffi_import` with its re-export. The later stages empty the regions part by part: an
item's C layout and C owners leave `ffi_import` with its `port/layout` and `port/memory`,
its export leaves `ffi_export` with its `port/unexport`. A module without either region is
native, and its file carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

## 3. Anchors

The Rust item that stands in for each C item is annotated, and those annotations are the
only record that an item was translated.

An annotation is two attributes on the same Rust item, a doc-comment anchor and a rustdoc
alias:

```rust
/// Wraps `fn::git_repository_open`
#[doc(alias = "git_repository_open")]
pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<RepositoryBox, Error> { … }
```

| anchor | meaning |
|---|---|
| ``/// Wraps `<kind>::<path>` `` | safe view over the FFI seam |
| ``/// Replaces `<kind>::<path>` `` | native Rust translation |

The anchor's path is a code span, in backticks, as rustdoc renders it and as the
workspace's `clippy::doc_markdown` lint requires of a path in a doc comment.

`<path>` names the item as its batch schedules it, and `<kind>` says what it is:

| kind | item |
|---|---|
| `fn` | a function |
| `st` | a struct |
| `un` | a union |
| `enm` | an enum, or one of its constants |
| `fnp` | a function pointer |
| `tdf` | a typedef: one of its own, or one an item lists among its `typedefs` |
| `fld` | a member of a struct or union |
| `glb` | a global |
| `mac` | a macro |

A path is made of names only: the names the source resolves the item by, outermost first,
separated by `.`, as the source language scopes them. A function, a type, an enum's
constant, a global, a typedef or a function pointer a typedef declares is its own name,
since C scopes a constant as it does its enum. A member is its struct's or union's path
followed by the member's name, and a member of a member continues the path, as
`fld::AVOption.default_val.i64`. A function pointer written inline is its declaring site's
path: a member's, `<function>.<param>` for a parameter, `<function>.return` for a return,
or a global's name. An element without a name adds no step to the paths of what it holds:

- an anonymous struct or union held by a named member is reached through that member, so
  its members are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`;
- the members of an unnamed struct or union member, such as C11's anonymous members, are
  named as members of the type that holds it, as the source reaches them; and
- an array's elements are reached without an index, so the members of an array member's
  element type are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`.

An element without a name has no annotation of its own. The Rust item that stands in for
it is annotated with the named member that holds it, or, when it is held by no name, with
each member it stands in for. A type declared inside another is named as its language
scopes it: a C struct tag has file scope, so a struct declared inside another is still
`st::<tag>`. An enum without a name has no annotation of its own, and its constants keep
theirs.

The alias is the bare `<path>`, without the backticks, so that a consumer who searches the
documentation for the source's name finds every item that stands in for it. The kind is
the anchor's alone: a label in the alias would no longer match that search. An item whose
own name is that path, a name of the source the Rust keeps, carries no alias: rustdoc
rejects an alias equal to its item's name, and the name already answers the search. Its
anchor is unchanged.

### 3.1 What is annotated

The annotation goes on the public item a consumer uses in place of the C item, which is
not necessarily the item that makes the FFI call:

- a function: the function or method the public API exports, which a consumer imports
  instead of the FFI function. The private helper that makes the call, an `ffi_export`
  gateway and a test are not annotated.
- a lifecycle routine, raw, typed or string: the method of the public lifecycle trait the
  strategy implements, such as `CDrop::c_drop`, where it is handwritten, or the macro
  invocation that mints it, which passes the annotation to the method. Again, the method
  annotated need not be the one making the unsafe call.
- a type: the layout newtype that defines the FFI type, handwritten or minted by
  `define_ctype!`.
- a union: the tagged enum that stands in for it at every use.
- an enum: the Rust enum or newtype that stands in for it, and each of its constants: the
  variant or the constant that stands in for it.
- a macro: the generic, `const`, function or `macro_rules!` that stands in for it; a type
  generator's instances keep their own kinds, on the aliases.
- a function pointer: the callable type that stands in for it, or the trait, for a struct
  of function pointers.
- a typedef: the alias that stands in for it.
- a member: each of its accessors, the getter and the setter alike.

### 3.2 Several stand-ins

One C item may have several annotated Rust items, each carrying the same anchor and
alias: the ownership variants one C function is split into when one signature cannot
express every valid contract, as [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Functions section describes, and the accessors of one field. That is the only case in which an
annotation is duplicated. Existing annotations are completed work unless the current
objective deliberately promotes their item: a port of an item a binding wraps, or the
`port/layout` that gives a wrapped struct or union its native layout, replaces its `Wraps`
anchor with a `Replaces` one, and keeps its alias.

## 4. Testing

Tests are placed by what they target. Tests of the public interface are Cargo integration
tests of the safe crate, under `tests/`, so crate privacy enforces
the public-interface boundary. Each suite's `main.rs` declares one module per tested
translation unit, in `<suite>/<the tested TU>.rs`.

- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the safe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_safe`, whose `main.rs` carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Those the compiler
  should reject are placed in `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the unsafe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_unsafe`.
- Tests that compare the module's exported API with C's are placed in `tests/equiv_pub`,

# Testing builds

The builds every test of [`testing`](../SKILL.md) runs against, and how coverage is measured
over them.

## 1. Builds

Tests run against the target's prebuilt, immutable builds, recorded as the `variants` of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`: each an out-of-tree `dir` and the `configure` and `build`
commands run from it, its `version` raised whenever a command changes. They are:

- `plain`, the functional baseline;
- `coverage`, the coverage-instrumented build for campaign measurements, instrumented as
  [Coverage](#2-coverage) describes; and
- one variant per sanitizer the campaign enables, whose tests build the Rust with the same
  LLVM sanitizer as the C, the C's clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version as for
  coverage, so that one runtime serves both and a report from the Rust's own unsafe code is
  caught too, and whose C consumers that link the safe crate's Rust static library, from a
  module's switch on, link one built with the same instrumentation:
  - `asan-ubsan`, the general build, which FFI and lifecycle tests use;
  - `msan`, which instruments every component, the standard library included;
  - `tsan`, separate from `asan-ubsan`, since ASan and TSan instrument the same memory
    operations and their runtimes conflict; and
  - `bsan`, when BorrowSanitizer's `bsan` toolchain is installed and answers its version;
    it instruments the C through its own matched clang.

A Rust- or bindgen-only change reuses a matching variant: same C revision, `build.json`
version, compiler and instrumentation. Nothing writes into a variant's `dir`: each run's
logs and outputs go to paths of its own. A change to the compiled target, or no matching
variant, needs a private build, which the raw bindings link when `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR` names
it in place of a variant, and the shared variants are rebuilt once that change lands.

## 2. Coverage

Coverage is counted with one instrument for C and Rust, so that a C figure and a Rust
figure, and the campaign's figures and those of a crate it is compared with, are counted
alike, and count the code under test only:

- **Instrumentation.** The `coverage` variant compiles the C with clang's source-based
  coverage, `-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping` in its compile and link flags,
  from a clang of the pinned nightly's LLVM major version, and the Rust is compiled on that
  nightly with `-C instrument-coverage`. One profiling runtime counts both, into a profile
  per process and module (`LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=<dir>/%p-%m.profraw`), and the nightly's
  `llvm-profdata` and `llvm-cov` read both. gcc's coverage instrumentation and gcov are not used: their
  lines follow the line table of the optimized code, which the optimization level changes,
  so their figures cannot be compared with Rust's.
- **Test code.** Test code is not instrumented, so it is neither credited as covered nor
  counted as code to cover. Counted, it would inflate the suite that runs it, whose own
  lines run whenever it does, and deflate every other suite, whose denominator would hold
  lines it never runs. Every test item of the measured crate, under `#[test]`,
  `#[cfg(test)]` or a `cfg` that requires `test`, carries `#[coverage(off)]`, which covers
  everything nested in it, and the crate root enables `#![feature(coverage_attribute)]`.
  The attributes are added in a scratch copy of the measured tree under `crustify/tmp/`,
  which is measured in its place, so that the measured crates are not changed. Integration
  test crates, examples, benches, the crate root's build script and the generated raw
  bindings under `sys/` are left out of the report by path. Test code that is not an item, such as a `#[cfg(test)]`
  block inside a library function, stays instrumented, and is reported with the figures.
- **Objects.** C coverage is read from the objects the tests load: the variant's shared
  libraries, or the object files a crate links statically, every TU compiled into them
  counting, and one no test reaches at zero. A figure covers the sources of the library it
  names, selected by directory, so that the copies of its inline functions and of its TUs
  that other libraries compile, the configuration headers the build generates and the C's
  own tests count toward none. Rust coverage is read from every test and doctest binary of
  the crate. All objects are passed for every suite, so that every suite has the same
  denominator.
- **Suites.** Each suite runs alone, into its own profile directory, merged into one
  profile; the total merges the suites' profiles, so it is their union, never their sum.
  Doctests are a suite of their own.
- **Figures.** The figures are the totals `llvm-cov report` prints, unmodified: line,
  function and region coverage, line coverage leading. Its per-line views (`llvm-cov show`
  and the LCOV export) count lines differently, marking the bodies of C macro definitions
  as executed: they locate gaps, and never compute a figure.
- **Comparisons.** A crate the campaign is compared with is measured the same way: its
  test items marked in a scratch copy, its own release of the C built as the `coverage`
  variant is, its suites run alone, and its figures read from `llvm-cov report`. A
  comparison names its scope, and both sides are measured over the same one.

### 2.1 A worklist's coverage

A worklist's tests run against the campaign's `coverage` variant, measured as
above, and coverage is inspected for the C and Rust execution
paths belonging to the worklist. Focused tests are added to cover its reachable uncovered
paths. Paths that remain uncovered because they are unreachable, environment-dependent, or
intentionally nondeterministic are reported as such.

Coverage is maximized, not gated. Each worklist reports its regions and branches beside
its lines, and which of its types' states and transitions, as the analysis lists them, its
tests reach. In a port, a module's C is the reference until its switch: its coverage
under the module's equivalence tests shows how much of its behaviour they compare, set
against what its own C tests reach. From the switch on, the module's coverage is its
Rust's.

description: "Naming, tree layout, anchors and test placement of the Rust a campaign generates. Read before writing, homing or reviewing generated Rust or tests."

# Crustify coding conventions

These are the shared, mechanical contracts of the code a campaign generates: how it is
named, where it sits, how it records what it translated and where its tests go. The
toolchain, edition, lints and formatting it is held to are [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Naming

The workspace's lints enforce the standard Rust casing below, as [`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s
Lints section describes.

The safe surface uses ordinary Rust naming: `snake_case` for functions, methods and
modules, `UpperCamelCase` for types and traits, `SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE` for constants and
statics. A C name's library or owning-type prefix is dropped wherever the crate, module or
receiver already supplies it, and the idiomatic Rust term is preferred over a
transliterated C one. The filled anchor records the C name, so renaming costs no
traceability. Names that cross the language boundary keep their C-derived spelling, as
below.

### 1.1 Functions

A C function's raw binding is `sys::<name>`. Its safe wrapper is a free function homed in
the owning module, named by the rules above. When one C function has several valid
ownership contracts, each safe variant has a distinct, descriptive name.

### 1.2 Types

A wrapped C type is the layout-compatible newtype `Foo`, named by the rules above; its
shared and exclusive borrowed handles are `FooRef<'a>` and `FooMut<'a>`, and its sole and
counted owners `FooBox` and `FooArc`. A port keeps these names while what they name
changes, as [`porting-types`](../porting/types/SKILL.md)'s Structs section describes. A typedef that
names a type under another name, which its item lists among its `typedefs`, is a
`pub type` alias of the type's Rust form.

A function pointer a typedef declares is named after its typedef. One written inline is
named after the site that declares it, its holder's name followed by its own and `Fn`: a
field's `<Struct><Field>Fn`, a parameter's `<Function><Param>Fn`, a return's
`<Function>ReturnFn` and a global's `<Global>Fn`.

### 1.3 Shims

A callable macro shim is `crustify_<NAME>`.

### 1.4 Exports

Each ported module has one raw ABI gateway, its `ffi_export` region, as
[Unsafe regions](#21-unsafe-regions) describes, whose exports use `#[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C"` under the bare C names: the
module's functions and globals that C outside the module references, another module's TU
or a C test or executable that stays, the `static inline` functions its headers define
included. The exports serve that C, which reaches the module through them once it has
switched. A function or global only the module's own C references is not exported: that
C leaves the build with the module at its switch, and its callers are Rust from then
on; nor are static functions and static globals, which nothing outside their TU reaches.
The target's public C API, for C outside the target, is deferred: exports serve the
target's own remaining C alone, and that API is a layer of its own over the native Rust API,
added once the modules it covers are ported.
<!-- TODO: that layer, a C-compatible ABI over the ported public API, is not specified
yet. Until it is, a C consumer outside the target does not survive a port. -->
An export is removed, with the raw binding that reaches it, by its symbol's `port/unexport`,
after the switch that removes the last C that calls it, takes its address or
accesses it. A C test tied to the module that stays, using only its public API, does not
hold an export back: it checks the export while other C needs it, and leaves with it.

### 1.5 Export features

Each module's `ffi_export` is compiled only under the safe crate's Cargo feature
`ffi-export-<tu>`, with `<tu>` its translation unit's path below the C root, every character
that is not an ASCII letter or digit replaced by `-`. The feature is off until the module
switches, so that its exports never collide with the C they replace, and the switch
deletes it, its gateway compiling unconditionally from then on.

## 2. Crates, modules, and TUs

The Rust tree is the repository's own, as [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Tree section lays it
out, all relative to the repository's root:

- `Cargo.toml` - the safe crate's manifest, which also declares the workspace.
- `src/lib.rs` - the safe crate's root, with one `cfg`-gated module per link unit.
- `src/<link-unit>/` - one sub-dir per link unit.
- `src/sys.rs` and `sys/<link-unit>/` - the raw bindings, one public module per link unit,
  laid out as [`bindgen`](../bindgen/SKILL.md) describes.

The safe crate is named after its repository, `<repo>-crustify`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section names it:
a name crates.io leaves free, which tells it apart from the source's own Rust bindings,
such as `git2` for libgit2.

Within a link unit's sub-dir, the tree follows the module decomposition in `modules.json`
exactly, and preserves the C layout as far as the idiomatic organization of a Rust tree
allows:

- each module is one `.rs` file, at its translation unit's path below the C root with the
  `.rs` extension: its TU and the headers bundled with it have no files of their own,
  since Rust has no headers;
- a header module is one `<stem>_h.rs` file, at its header's path;
- the two modules of a split foundational TU share the TU's file;
- C directories become Rust modules: a directory's `.rs` file sits beside the directory,
  as `<dir>.rs` and `<dir>/`, and declares the modules within it, or is the module of a TU
  with the directory's name where there is one; `mod.rs` files are not used; and
- a file or directory name that is not a Rust identifier is sanitized, hyphens to
  underscores, and a Rust keyword takes a trailing underscore.

Where a C layout has no idiomatic Rust counterpart, the tree adapts it in the conventional
Rust way and keeps the C path recognizable. A batch names the `.rs` file each of its items
belongs in, as `src/<link-unit>/…/<file>.rs`. Entities sharing a
definition site co-home. A home may be shared across waves.

### 2.1 Unsafe regions

A module's unsafe code is confined to at most two inline child modules of its file, its
unsafe regions, so that the rest of the file, its native code, holds none:

- `mod ffi_import`: what the module reaches in C: its calls through the raw bindings, the C
  layouts it wraps with their handles and accessors, the owners and lifecycle policies over
  C's allocator, and the trampolines and contexts through which C calls a Rust closure
  back; and
- `mod ffi_export { use super::*; … }`: the gateway through which C reaches the module by
  symbol, as [Exports](#14-exports) describes, compiled only under its
  [export feature](#15-export-features).

Unsafe code is every `unsafe` block, `unsafe fn`, `unsafe impl`, `unsafe extern` block and
`#[unsafe(…)]` attribute, and every invocation of another crate's macro that expands to
one, such as one that mints a type over a C layout, which the compiler's `unsafe_code` lint does not
see. Outside the regions, only the raw bindings hold any. The regions take the lint back as
[`toolchain`](../toolchain/SKILL.md)'s Unsafe code section describes.

A region exposes to its module only what [`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary
section lets it expose, and the module re-exports the public items a region defines, as
`pub use ffi_import::{Foo, FooBox, FooMut, FooRef};`, so that their paths do not depend on
which side defines them. A type's inherent `impl` blocks may be split between the native
code and a region: each method is visible as its own visibility says, counted from the
module that holds its block, so that a region's private helpers stay hidden from the
native code.

A region exists only while it holds something. A wrap's items are in `ffi_import`. A port
writes its item in the native code, and keeps in the regions only the C form the item
keeps, as [`porting`](../porting/SKILL.md) describes; a wrapped item it ports leaves
`ffi_import` with its re-export. The later stages empty the regions part by part: an
item's C layout and C owners leave `ffi_import` with its `port/layout` and `port/memory`,
its export leaves `ffi_export` with its `port/unexport`. A module without either region is
native, and its file carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`.

## 3. Anchors

The Rust item that stands in for each C item is annotated, and those annotations are the
only record that an item was translated.

An annotation is two attributes on the same Rust item, a doc-comment anchor and a rustdoc
alias:

```rust
/// Wraps `fn::git_repository_open`
#[doc(alias = "git_repository_open")]
pub fn open(path: &Path) -> Result<RepositoryBox, Error> { … }
```

| anchor | meaning |
|---|---|
| ``/// Wraps `<kind>::<path>` `` | safe view over the FFI seam |
| ``/// Replaces `<kind>::<path>` `` | native Rust translation |

The anchor's path is a code span, in backticks, as rustdoc renders it and as the
workspace's `clippy::doc_markdown` lint requires of a path in a doc comment.

`<path>` names the item as its batch schedules it, and `<kind>` says what it is:

| kind | item |
|---|---|
| `fn` | a function |
| `st` | a struct |
| `un` | a union |
| `enm` | an enum, or one of its constants |
| `fnp` | a function pointer |
| `tdf` | a typedef: one of its own, or one an item lists among its `typedefs` |
| `fld` | a member of a struct or union |
| `glb` | a global |
| `mac` | a macro |

A path is made of names only: the names the source resolves the item by, outermost first,
separated by `.`, as the source language scopes them. A function, a type, an enum's
constant, a global, a typedef or a function pointer a typedef declares is its own name,
since C scopes a constant as it does its enum. A member is its struct's or union's path
followed by the member's name, and a member of a member continues the path, as
`fld::AVOption.default_val.i64`. A function pointer written inline is its declaring site's
path: a member's, `<function>.<param>` for a parameter, `<function>.return` for a return,
or a global's name. An element without a name adds no step to the paths of what it holds:

- an anonymous struct or union held by a named member is reached through that member, so
  its members are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`;
- the members of an unnamed struct or union member, such as C11's anonymous members, are
  named as members of the type that holds it, as the source reaches them; and
- an array's elements are reached without an index, so the members of an array member's
  element type are `fld::<path>.<member>.<inner>`.

An element without a name has no annotation of its own. The Rust item that stands in for
it is annotated with the named member that holds it, or, when it is held by no name, with
each member it stands in for. A type declared inside another is named as its language
scopes it: a C struct tag has file scope, so a struct declared inside another is still
`st::<tag>`. An enum without a name has no annotation of its own, and its constants keep
theirs.

The alias is the bare `<path>`, without the backticks, so that a consumer who searches the
documentation for the source's name finds every item that stands in for it. The kind is
the anchor's alone: a label in the alias would no longer match that search. An item whose
own name is that path, a name of the source the Rust keeps, carries no alias: rustdoc
rejects an alias equal to its item's name, and the name already answers the search. Its
anchor is unchanged.

### 3.1 What is annotated

The annotation goes on the public item a consumer uses in place of the C item, which is
not necessarily the item that makes the FFI call:

- a function: the function or method the public API exports, which a consumer imports
  instead of the FFI function. The private helper that makes the call, an `ffi_export`
  gateway and a test are not annotated.
- a lifecycle routine, raw, typed or string: the method of the public lifecycle trait the
  strategy implements, such as `CDrop::c_drop`, where it is handwritten, or the macro
  invocation that mints it, which passes the annotation to the method. Again, the method
  annotated need not be the one making the unsafe call.
- a type: the layout newtype that defines the FFI type, handwritten or minted by
  `define_ctype!`.
- a union: the tagged enum that stands in for it at every use.
- an enum: the Rust enum or newtype that stands in for it, and each of its constants: the
  variant or the constant that stands in for it.
- a macro: the generic, `const`, function or `macro_rules!` that stands in for it; a type
  generator's instances keep their own kinds, on the aliases.
- a function pointer: the callable type that stands in for it, or the trait, for a struct
  of function pointers.
- a typedef: the alias that stands in for it.
- a member: each of its accessors, the getter and the setter alike.

### 3.2 Several stand-ins

One C item may have several annotated Rust items, each carrying the same anchor and
alias: the ownership variants one C function is split into when one signature cannot
express every valid contract, as [`binding-symbols`](../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Functions section describes, and the accessors of one field. That is the only case in which an
annotation is duplicated. Existing annotations are completed work unless the current
objective deliberately promotes their item: a port of an item a binding wraps, or the
`port/layout` that gives a wrapped struct or union its native layout, replaces its `Wraps`
anchor with a `Replaces` one, and keeps its alias.

## 4. Testing

Tests are placed by what they target. Tests of the public interface are Cargo integration
tests of the safe crate, under `tests/`, so crate privacy enforces
the public-interface boundary. Each suite's `main.rs` declares one module per tested
translation unit, in `<suite>/<the tested TU>.rs`.

- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the safe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_safe`, whose `main.rs` carries `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`. Those the compiler
  should reject are placed in `tests/ub_safe/compile_fail/`.
- Tests that target undefined behaviour on the unsafe public interface are placed in
  `tests/ub_unsafe`.
- Tests that compare the module's exported API with C's are placed in `tests/equiv_pub`,
  and those that compare its internals with C's in an inline `#[cfg(test)] mod equiv_priv`
  beside the unit they test.
- Tests that check the public interface through Rust assertions are placed in
  `tests/unit_pub`, and those that check internal routines in an inline
  `#[cfg(test)] mod unit_priv` beside the unit they test.

An inline test of a region's code sits in that region, and an inline test that holds
unsafe code, such as an `equiv_priv` test calling the C, sits in a region: the module's
`ffi_import`, for the C it calls. The suites whose tests call the raw bindings or the public unsafe API,
`tests/ub_unsafe` and `tests/equiv_pub`, take `unsafe_code` back at their `main.rs`, as a
region does.

A standalone reproducer is not a test: it is placed with the report that cites it.

---
name: testing
description: "How work is tested: test kinds and suites, test objects, how thoroughly a wrapper is tested, UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, equivalence and unit tests, and the C tests carried over; testing-builds and testing-gates give the builds, coverage and gates. Read before writing tests."
---

# Testing

Tests are classified by what decides them and by the side of a module they test, and each
is placed where the conventions' Testing section places tests of its kind:

- UB tests on the safe public interface show that it does not reach UB, mainly by not
  triggering sanitizer or Miri crashes, or by failing to compile for a given illegal path;
- UB tests on the unsafe public interface target UB there: each public `unsafe fn` or
  method a workset adds, called within its stated `# Safety` contract, edge cases
  included. Raw `sys::` round-trips are not UB tests on the unsafe interface; they are unit
  or equivalence tests;
- equivalence tests show that the Rust behaves as the C it translates, mainly by passing
  equivalence assertions: `equiv_pub` on the module's exported API, `equiv_priv` on its
  internals; and
- unit tests show that the Rust keeps its contract, by passing Rust assertions, without
  the C: `unit_pub` on the public interface, `unit_priv` on the internal routines.

<!-- TODO: fuzzing, of the safe public interface and differentially against the C, is
deferred. -->

Test objects are constructed through safe constructors. The UB tests on the safe public
interface use the safe API alone, their suite forbidding `unsafe_code` at its root: a type
that no safe constructor or producer yields yet gets those tests in the batch that wraps
its first one. Elsewhere, while a type has no safe constructor, one documented unsafe
fixture per type adopts the raw constructor's result, and is replaced once the safe
constructor exists.

A test exercises the safe API wherever it can, so that the later stages of a port, which
keep that API, keep it passing. A test of a C form an item keeps, such as an unsafe
adoption, a function pointer's unsafe constructor, a trampoline or an export, goes with
the stage that removes the form.

How thoroughly a wrapper is tested follows how long it lasts. One a port will replace, a
type wrapped ahead of its port or a dependency whose module will be ported, keeps its safe
API through the port: it gets the tests of its public interface, which outlive it, and
none of its internals. A permanent one, every wrapper of a wrap campaign, the foundational
modules' and one whose later stage is held back for good, gets every kind.

The builds the tests run against and how coverage is measured are
[`testing-builds`](builds/SKILL.md)'s, and the gates every landing passes
[`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. UB tests

UB tests show that a workset's public API is free of UB.

The unsafe public interface is tested with one suite per public unsafe function or method
a workset adds, its inputs built through the safe API wherever one exists. A workset that
adds no public unsafe API has no UB tests on the unsafe interface.

The sanitizers available are those the campaign built: the instrumented variants of
`crustify/artifacts/build.json`, where `asan-ubsan` provides ASan and UBSan, `msan` MSan, `tsan` TSan
and `bsan` BSan. A sanitizer without a variant is not available, so no test is written for
it and none runs under it. Miri needs no C build and is always available.

A target that ships its own sanitizers, because the standard ones cannot run against it,
is tested with those instead, each standing for the sanitizer it implements.

Each available sanitizer is a separate obligation of an item while it reaches C or unsafe
code; once it reaches neither, as a port's later stages bring about, Miri covers it alone:

- ASan/UBSan: bounds errors, use-after-free, use-after-return, invalid free, double free,
  pointer/alignment UB, and integer/division/shift UB.
- MSan: use of uninitialized memory, including branches and addresses computed from it,
  uninitialized bytes crossing the FFI boundary, and struct tails or buffers a foreign
  initializer left partly unwritten. Its build instruments every component, the standard
  library through `-Zbuild-std` included: memory written by uninstrumented code reads as
  uninitialized, so a partial build reports falsely.
- BSan: conflicting foreign writes and retained foreign pointers across Rust reborrows.
  These tests are written like the others. BSan is the slowest instrument and reports
  false positives at the foreign boundary, so it runs only as
  [`testing-gates`](gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions section describes.
- TSan: races reachable through safe APIs, including every asserted `Send` or `Sync`
  implementation and threaded callback.
- Miri: Rust-side lifetime, bounds, initialization, validity, alignment, intrinsic, and
  `repr` assumptions. Miri cannot call the foreign library, read its globals or spawn a
  process, so every test that cannot run under it carries
  `#[cfg_attr(miri, ignore = "<reason>")]` on its test function, naming what stops it:
  `"calls C"`, `"reads a C global"`, and so on. A test is marked only after it was run
  alone under Miri and seen to stop there; never to silence a Miri report of undefined
  behaviour, a panic or a failed assertion, which are findings. The mark goes once what it
  names no longer stops the test, as a module's switch or a later stage brings about. Neither
  `#[cfg(not(miri))]` nor test-name filters stand in for the attribute: with it in place,
  Miri runs every other test.

A leak is not undefined behaviour, in Rust or in C, so neither a LeakSanitizer report,
which ASan's runtime makes by default, nor Miri's leak check is a UB candidate.

UB tests exercise every owner and borrowed form, shared and mutable access path, lifecycle
strategy, generic instance, and callback variant a batch emits. They attempt to outlive the
owner, alias a reborrow, reenter a callback, and drop a parent first. Storage that C and
Rust both allocate or free, or whose allocator a port moves, is tested for a free through
the wrong allocator.

When the type system should reject a program, the test is a compile-fail doctest or a
`trybuild` case.

## 2. Equivalence tests

Equivalence tests run the C and the Rust that translates it on independently owned inputs
built from one description, and compare:

- return values and errors;
- out-parameters and buffers;
- callbacks;
- state transitions; and
- lifecycle effects.

They use multi-call sequences and compare after each step; single calls are only a
baseline.

The C side of a test meets the preconditions the C sets its callers, as the wrapper meets
them before its own calls: a library's global initialisation, which writes state its
routines read without synchronisation, runs before the test's first call that reads it,
since the harness runs other tests beside it on other threads.

They compare what the C specifies, through the mapping the safe API applies to it, such as
its status returns as errors and its null pointers as absent values, and not what it leaves

  equivalence assertions: `equiv_pub` on the module's exported API, `equiv_priv` on its
  internals; and
- unit tests show that the Rust keeps its contract, by passing Rust assertions, without
  the C: `unit_pub` on the public interface, `unit_priv` on the internal routines.

keep that API, keep it passing. A test of a C form an item keeps, such as an unsafe
adoption, a function pointer's unsafe constructor, a trampoline or an export, goes with

type wrapped ahead of its port or a dependency whose module will be ported, keeps its safe

adds no public unsafe API has no UB tests on the unsafe interface.

content.content:
---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document
its tool skill names, read in full before the first change to the tool: they keep what the
tool is from drifting, such as an analysis that stays syntactic and does no data-flow
analysis. A change that departs from one of them is proposed, not made, and says so. A
tool with no such document has every change that alters what it is, rather than fixing or
extending what it does, proposed, not made.
<!-- TODO: ffimap has no goals document yet. -->

## 2. Signals

Evolution starts from evidence a campaign produces, never from taste:

| signal | what it suggests |
|---|---|
| a tool that crashes, or reports what the source contradicts | a defect in the tool |
| skills that contradict each other, or an agent prompt that leads its agent wrong | a defect in the spec |
| a rule an agent works around, or that forces a worse result than its omission would | an overconstraining rule, loosened or removed |
| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

A proposal needs one of these, with its evidence: a defect, a failure, a recurring
finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

A rule an agent cannot follow because its host refuses it, a write or a tool call
blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

The test between a lesson and the spec is generality: a rule that can only be stated in
the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

The campaign keeps an index of its proposals, `crustify/evolution/INDEX.md`, one row per
proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

A signal is filed once while its proposal waits. Before a run files a proposal, it reads the
index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: open proposals are landed
as the autonomy allows, the working branches are offered to the user for `devel`, and the
revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled. The
lessons are reconciled when [Lessons](#5-lessons) times it, and the record's rows are read
when [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) times it.

## 11. The record

The record of what landed, `EVOLUTION.md`, and how evolution itself evolves from it are
[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

content.content:
## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.
## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
