## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.
## 1. The dashboard

The dashboard, `crustify/artifacts/dashboard.md` unless the settings name another, is the
campaign's record of what each planner run, batch, wave and module did and cost. It is
filled from `templates/translate/dashboard.template.md`, an audit's from
`templates/audit/dashboard.template.md`, and keeps the template's format exactly.
When an adopted Crustify change adds a table or a column to the template, it is
added to the dashboard on the working branch before the next batch launches: a batch
fills the rows of the tables in place, and never adds one.

It is tracked in the campaign's tree, so every agent's worktree holds a copy, and it is
filled as the work lands rather than at the end. Each figure is measured once, where it is
produced: no suite or scan is rerun only to record one.

## 2. Cells

The dashboard's cells fall into three kinds, by when their figures can be known.

### 2.1 Landing cells

The cells measured on the tree a landing commits:

- for a batch, under the route its items' `kind` selects, as
  [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Routes section gives it: its rows
  in that route's `Batches`, tests, `Batches: safety audit` and `Batches: API stability` tables, and for a review batch in
  `Batches — review: PoC + reports`, each placed in module, wave and batch order under
  its `pass`, and for a module pass, which spans both routes, in `Module passes`; those
  tables' `Σ` rows; and the `Coverage stats` table and the Overview's LoC
  line;
- for a planner run, its row in `Planning`, but for its usage cells.

They are filled in the landing's last commit, and measured against the integration branch
tip it was rebased onto: coverage as [`testing-builds`](../../verification/testing/builds/SKILL.md)'s Coverage section measures
it, the safety audit columns as the changes in the dashboard's Safety audit metrics, and
the API stability columns as the changes to the API of the landing's items are classified. A
rebase that conflicts in the dashboard keeps every row both sides added, and the landing's
cells, `Σ` rows included, are measured again where the gates its rebase reruns cover them;
the others stand as measured on the batch's base.

An integration merge, and any merge of one branch into another, keeps every row both
sides added, and settles the rest so: an additive `Σ` cell is the sum over the merged
rows, ours plus theirs less the merge base's, and so are the Overview's `Rust LoC`
figures; a usage `Σ` cell, its per-unit cells included, sums only the rows that carry
usage, so that it is filled again with theirs; a coverage `Σ` cell, and the Overview's
`C LoC`, are the later landing's; and `Coverage stats` takes the merged suites' counts,
with the later landing's percentages until a gate measures the merged tree, which the
merge commit's message says. A table or section the template holds once is kept once,
with the rows of every copy, whether or not the merge conflicts there, and the merged
dashboard is checked for repeated headings before it is committed.

## Binding and porting

### Binding › Safe boundary

Before a batch lands, a scan with `--sites fn.unsafe.pub raw_ptr.field.pub
raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub` lists the public
`unsafe fn`s and the raw pointers on the safe public interface, and each of those sites
that belongs to the batch's changeset and that a safe variant could replace is fixed.
Its `--sites` also name the unsafe code outside both regions,
`code.unsafe_block.of_which.outside_regions`, another crate's macro expansions included,
which the `unsafe_code` lint misses, and `fn.unsafe.of_which.outside_regions.pub` and
`.priv`: outside the raw bindings, each of those sites in the batch's changeset is moved
into its region.

## Accounting

### Accounting › Landing cells

A batch's row in the dashboard's `Batches: safety audit` table is the change in each of
the Safety audit's metrics, from a scan of the tip its landing rebased onto to a scan of
the tree it lands.

### Accounting › API stability

`ffimap api` measures a safe crate's consumer-facing API per C item, from rustdoc JSON, as
its `docs/api.md` describes, read in full before its first use. A C item is the
`<kind>::<path>` of a `Wraps` or `Replaces` anchor, its surface every stand-in the anchor
names and the handles and owners tied to it, each judged by the contract
[`binding-types`](../../rust/binding/types/SKILL.md)' Safe layout section gives a consumer:
the methods every form offers, its reborrows and dereferences, and the traits a consumer
can use, never a form's raw access or seams. A batch generates the safe crate's rustdoc
JSON on the tip its landing rebased onto and on the tree it lands, with a nightly whose
`format_version` the tool supports, and ffibox's, with private items, for the contracts of
the forms it defines:

```bash
cargo +<nightly> rustdoc -p <crate> --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json
ffimap api diff <base>.json <tree>.json --dep <ffibox>.json --items "<the worklist's keys>" --format json
```

Each item comes out `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed` or `new`, with its anchor's
move from `Wraps` to `Replaces` where a port made it. The batch's row in the dashboard's
`Batches: API stability` table counts them over its worklist, and over the crate's
unattributed public items, compared per module.

### Accounting › Records

An unseeded scan of the unsafe and FFI surface is recorded at each batch's, wave's and
the campaign's end, as `ffimap.json` in its artifact directory: a batch's in the run dir
of the run that landed it, a wave's in its wave's dir, as `layout` spells it, and the
campaign's in `crustify/artifacts/`. A module's end is the scan of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

A review locates the sites of its objectives with a scan, `--sites` with their counters,
and keeps those in its workset: the code its commits add or change, or its modules and
the types, trait impls and functions they name. The sites are where the reading starts,
as [`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s Worklists section describes; an
audit's review is the same review with no scan at all.

- `unsafety`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`.
- `contracts`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, whose `# Safety` obligations are evaluated.
- `ub`: these smells first, in this order:
  1. references into C memory: the references to a cell outside its sanctioned positions,
     `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}` less those shares, and to a raw C
     struct, `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, then
     `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`;
  2. thread-safety claims, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and
     `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`, checked against
     the C library's contract: a data race is reachable from safe code when the library
     does not allow what they assert;
  3. the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, found in the source: unsound when the
     handle can outlive the owner of the memory or the point at which C frees or
     invalidates it;
  4. raw pointers a consumer can set, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
     `raw_ptr.field.pub`, with their `of_which.void` shares: unsound when a safe path
     dereferences or frees what the consumer passed or stored;
  5. raw-pointer dereferences, `raw_ptr.deref.wr` then `raw_ptr.deref.rd`: first in the
     modules that also hold references into C memory, where a write may invalidate a
     reference, and outside a type's accessors; and
  6. hand-written teardown and copies, `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}`
     and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`.

## Audit

### Audit workflow › Scope and priority

In an audit a scan is a hint. Where the settings' `tool-hints` answer allows one, it is
run once each build configuration is in place, with `--sites` over the counters of the
audit's objectives, and set beside the reading of the crate: a site the reading missed is
read, and a module the scan reports nothing in is planned and reviewed from its source
like any other. A scan decides neither what is in scope nor its order, and no workset is
dropped, deferred or reviewed more lightly for having no sites.

A scan that fails, that covers part of the crate, such as the files of one configuration,
or that the source contradicts stops nothing: the plan stands on the reading, and the
failure is proposed as ffimap's defect.

### Audit workflow › Worksets

A site of `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop`, `.impl_clone`,
`ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send` or `.sync`, at either leaf, is a trait impl, named
`Drop for <type>`, `Clone for <type>`, `Send for <type>` or `Sync for <type>`. A review
that scans does so over its own modules, so the sites are not passed on.

the forms it defines:

```bash
cargo +<nightly> rustdoc -p <crate> --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json
ffimap api diff <base>.json <tree>.json --dep <ffibox>.json --items "<the worklist's keys>" --format json
```

Each item comes out `kept`, `extended`, `changed`, `removed` or `new`, with its anchor's
move from `Wraps` to `Replaces` where a port made it. The batch's row in the dashboard's
`Batches: API stability` table counts them over its worklist, and over the crate's
unattributed public items, compared per module.

### Accounting › Records

An unseeded scan of the unsafe and FFI surface is recorded at each batch's, wave's and
the campaign's end, as `ffimap.json` in its artifact directory: a batch's in the run dir
of the run that landed it, a wave's in its wave's dir, as `layout` spells it, and the
campaign's in `crustify/artifacts/`. A module's end is the scan of the last wave of its `wrap` and `port` items.

## Reviewing

### Reviewing › Objectives

A review locates the sites of its objectives with a scan, `--sites` with their counters,
and keeps those in its workset: the code its commits add or change, or its modules and
the types, trait impls and functions they name. The sites are where the reading starts,
as [`reviewing`](../../verification/reviewing/SKILL.md)'s Worklists section describes; an
audit's review is the same review with no scan at all.

- `unsafety`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.field.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`.
- `contracts`: `fn.unsafe.pub`, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.unsafe.pub` and
  `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.unsafe.pub`, whose `# Safety` obligations are evaluated.
- `ub`: these smells first, in this order:
  1. references into C memory: the references to a cell outside its sanctioned positions,
     `ty.ffibox.wrapper.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}` less those shares, and to a raw C
     struct, `ty.ffibox.sys.as.borrowed.std.{pub,priv}`, then
     `raw_ptr.casted_to.std.{borrow,slice,string}`;
  2. thread-safety claims, `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send.{pub,priv}` and
     `ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.sync.{pub,priv}`, checked against
     the C library's contract: a data race is reachable from safe code when the library
     does not allow what they assert;
  3. the lifetimes formed inside `unsafe` blocks, found in the source: unsound when the
     handle can outlive the owner of the memory or the point at which C frees or
     invalidates it;
  4. raw pointers a consumer can set, `raw_ptr.fn_sig_arg.safe.pub` and
     `raw_ptr.field.pub`, with their `of_which.void` shares: unsound when a safe path
     dereferences or frees what the consumer passed or stored;
  5. raw-pointer dereferences, `raw_ptr.deref.wr` then `raw_ptr.deref.rd`: first in the
     modules that also hold references into C memory, where a write may invalidate a
     reference, and outside a type's accessors; and
  6. hand-written teardown and copies, `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop.{pub,priv}`
     and `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_clone.{pub,priv}`.

## Audit

### Audit workflow › Scope and priority

In an audit a scan is a hint. Where the settings' `tool-hints` answer allows one, it is
run once each build configuration is in place, with `--sites` over the counters of the
audit's objectives, and set beside the reading of the crate: a site the reading missed is
read, and a module the scan reports nothing in is planned and reviewed from its source
like any other. A scan decides neither what is in scope nor its order, and no workset is
dropped, deferred or reviewed more lightly for having no sites.

A scan that fails, that covers part of the crate, such as the files of one configuration,
or that the source contradicts stops nothing: the plan stands on the reading, and the
failure is proposed as ffimap's defect.

### Audit workflow › Worksets

A site of `ty.storing_raw_ptr.of_which.impl_drop`, `.impl_clone`,
`ty.impl_trait.of_which.std.send` or `.sync`, at either leaf, is a trait impl, named
`Drop for <type>`, `Clone for <type>`, `Send for <type>` or `Sync for <type>`. A review
that scans does so over its own modules, so the sites are not passed on.

#!/bin/bash
# Run cargo against one crustify prebuild of libgit2, instrumenting Rust to match.
#
#   crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]
#
# <variant> is a `variants` key of crustify/artifacts/build.json: plain, coverage, asan-ubsan,
# tsan or bsan. Each variant uses its own target dir under target/.
# The safe crate's build script, in campaign mode, links the variant's static archive (its
# `static` in build.json) into each test binary, so the C runs under the instrumentation the
# Rust is built with here, one runtime serving both. Set CRUSTIFY_BUILD_DIR to a private build
# of the variant, which carries the same archive, to link it instead of the shared one.
set -euo pipefail
variant=${1:?usage: cargo-variant.sh <variant> <cargo subcommand> [args...]}
shift
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../.." && pwd)
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=$variant
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=${CARGO_TARGET_DIR:-$here/target/$variant}
# pcre2-sys links the variant's side-campaign PCRE2, the one libgit2's C links, rather than
# building its vendored copy, which would shadow it in every test binary. The side campaigns'
# clones sit where the variant's build found their installs, beside the repository whose
# crustify/builds holds it (build.json's configure takes them from `$PWD/../../../..` in
# crustify/builds/<variant>): resolved physically through crustify/builds, which a worktree or
# a gate snapshot links to that repository's, so that every checkout finds the same ones.
side=$(realpath -m "$here/crustify/builds/$variant/../../../..")
export PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$side/pcre2-bindings/crustify/builds/$variant/install/lib/pkgconfig${PKG_CONFIG_PATH:+:$PKG_CONFIG_PATH}"
cd "$here"
# The nightly the workspace pins, for the sanitizers that need it.
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' Cargo.toml)
# Cargo's own flags must come before a `--`, which hands the rest to the test binaries.
pre=() post=()
for arg in "$@"; do
  if [ ${#post[@]} -gt 0 ] || [ "$arg" = -- ]; then post+=("$arg"); else pre+=("$arg"); fi
done
case $variant in
  plain)
    exec cargo "$@" ;;
  coverage)
    # Source-based coverage on the pinned nightly, against the variant's clang-instrumented C,
    # which each test binary links statically, so that rustc's profiler runtime counts both;
    # crustify/scripts/coverage/ measures the suites as the testing spec's Coverage section does.
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -C instrument-coverage"
    export LLVM_PROFILE_FILE=${LLVM_PROFILE_FILE:-$CARGO_TARGET_DIR/profraw/%p-%m.profraw}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  asan-ubsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address -Cforce-frame-pointers=yes"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=address"
    export ASAN_OPTIONS=${ASAN_OPTIONS:-detect_leaks=1:abort_on_error=1}
    export UBSAN_OPTIONS=${UBSAN_OPTIONS:-print_stacktrace=1:halt_on_error=1}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  tsan)
    export RUSTFLAGS="${RUSTFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    export RUSTDOCFLAGS="${RUSTDOCFLAGS:-} -Zsanitizer=thread"
    # glibc's tzset locks what TSan cannot see: see tsan.supp.
    export TSAN_OPTIONS=${TSAN_OPTIONS:-halt_on_error=1:suppressions=$here/crustify/scripts/tsan.supp}
    exec cargo "+$nightly" "${pre[@]}" -Zbuild-std --target $host "${post[@]}" ;;
  bsan)
    # trybuild's nested cargo build does not finish under BorrowSanitizer, and the
    # compile-fail suite is a compile-time check the plain variant already runs.
    # Under parallel test threads BorrowSanitizer's GC can take longer than its default
    # 10 s hang threshold to bring every thread to a safepoint, and then aborts; give it
    # 120 s rather than serialize the tests.
    export BSAN_OPTIONS=${BSAN_OPTIONS:-gc_hang_threshold_ms=120000}
    if [ "${1:-}" = test ]; then
      case " $* " in
        *" -- "*) exec cargo bsan "$@" --skip compile_fail ;;
        *) exec cargo bsan "$@" -- --skip compile_fail ;;
      esac
    fi
    exec cargo bsan "$@" ;;
  *)
    echo "unknown variant: $variant" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac

# `Entry`, `EntryRef` and `EntryMut` have no `Debug`

- **item**: `git_config_entry` (type), `crustify/rust/libgit2/libgit2/config/config.rs`
- **affected commit**: `512be0487` (libgit2/config wave 1 batch 0)
- **class**: misc (API ergonomics). The existing surface is sound.

## Finding

`define_ctype!` generates no `Debug`, and the batch added none. An `EntryArc` printed only
its pointer (ffibox's `CArc` `Debug`). Its `EntryRef` handle, which carries all six field
getters, did not implement `Debug` at all. So `{:?}` on an entry's fields, or a derived
`Debug` on a type holding an `EntryRef`, did not compile. Wave 3/4 will lend `EntryRef`s
to `git_config_foreach` callbacks and `git_config_next` iterators, where printing an entry
is the first thing a caller reaches for.

The config module's own `ConfigRef`/`ConfigMut`, and the options records reviewed in wave 0,
implement `Debug`.

## Fix

`Debug` for `EntryRef` prints the six fields through the getters (`name`, `value`,
`backend_type`, `origin_path`, `level`, `include_depth`), as `Entry { .. }`. `Entry` and
`EntryMut` delegate to it. Nothing reads beyond what the getters already read, so the
output borrows nothing and adds no unsafe code.

## Tests

`config.rs::unit_tests::debug_and_thread_traits` (Miri): an `EntryRef`, an `EntryMut` and
an inline `Entry` over a Rust-owned fixture print the expected string. The fixture
includes a NULL value and a non-UTF-8 origin.

# A spec is built one exclusive-handle setter at a time, where C writes one initialiser

- **finding**: `ergonomics/spec-built-one-setter-at-a-time`
- **batch**: `wave-186/batch-3/run-1`, the review of `wave-186/batch-0` (`8a149ac08`) and
  `wave-186/batch-2` (`fe6b85bfa`), `opt.h`'s types
- **items**: `st::cli_opt_spec`
- **affected commit**: `fe6b85bfa`
- **where**: `src/git2/src/cli/opt.rs`, `Spec::new` and `SpecMut`'s setters

## Finding

C declares a command's options as one array of initialisers, each spec where it is
declared, as `cmd_*.c` do (`c/src/cli/cmd_cat_file.c:25`):

```c
static const cli_opt_spec opts[] = {
	CLI_COMMON_OPT,

	{ CLI_OPT_TYPE_SWITCH,     NULL,    't', &display,    DISPLAY_TYPE,
	  CLI_OPT_USAGE_REQUIRED,  NULL,    "display the type of the object" },
	…
	{ 0 },
};
```

The wrap's safe API builds a spec from its `Target` alone (`Spec::new`). Every other field
takes a setter on the exclusive handle, reached through `as_mut()` on a mutable binding, so a
table must be declared `mut` and patched by index after it is built:

```rust
let mut specs = [Spec::new(Target::Bool(Some(&debug))), Spec::zeroed()];
specs[0].as_mut().set_name(Some(c"debug"));
specs[0].as_mut().set_alias(NonZero::new(b'd'));
specs[0].as_mut().set_help(Some(c"show debugging output"));
```

This is `reviewing`'s `ergonomics` objective: no builder where C takes a long argument list.
The spec has eight fields, and its consumers are the module's ported parser, its tests and
the CLI commands a port will bring to Rust, all of which declare tables. The batch's own
tests show the cost. `tests/equiv/src/cli/opt.rs` spent sixteen lines of
`specs[i].as_mut().set_…` on four tables, `tests/ub_safe/src/cli/opt.rs` four lines on two,
each spec's fields set apart from where the spec is declared. The alias also has to be
wrapped as `NonZero::new(b'd')`. The wrap is the first batch to give the struct a safe API,
which its `port/layout` keeps, so its ergonomics are reviewed here.

## Fix

`Spec<'p>` gains by-value builders in the module's native code: `with_name`, `with_alias`,
`with_switch_value`, `with_usage`, `with_value_name` and `with_help`. Each takes the spec and
returns it with one field set through its setter, and each is anchored to its field as its
setter is. `with_alias` takes the byte, `0` leaving the spec without an alias as C's `'\0'`
does. A spec now reads as its C initialiser does:

```rust
let specs = [
    Spec::new(Target::Bool(Some(&debug)))
        .with_name(c"debug")
        .with_alias(b'd')
        .with_help(c"show debugging output"),
    Spec::default(),

`Spec<'p>` gains by-value builders in the module's native code: `with_name`, `with_alias`,
`with_switch_value`, `with_usage`, `with_value_name` and `with_help`. Each takes the spec and

setter is. `with_alias` takes the byte, `0` leaving the spec without an alias as C's `'\0'`
does. A spec now reads as its C initialiser does:

==> crustify/scripts/coverage/baseline.sh <==
#!/bin/bash
# baseline.sh <crate checkout> <package> <cov dir> <nightly> [cargo test args...]: as run.sh, for a
# comparison crate: its own C built by its build script, instrumented through CC/CFLAGS.
set -uo pipefail
trap 'echo "failed at line $LINENO" >&2' ERR
src=$1 pkg=$2 out=$3 nightly=$4; shift 4
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
tree=$out/tree
rm -rf "$out"; mkdir -p "$tree" "$out/prof"
(cd "$src" && tar -cf - --exclude=./target --exclude=./.git .) | (cd "$tree" && tar -xf -)
# a scratch copy inside another workspace's tree is its own workspace
grep -q '^\[workspace\]' "$tree/Cargo.toml" || printf '\n[workspace]\n' >> "$tree/Cargo.toml"
root=$(cd "$tree" && cargo metadata --no-deps --format-version 1 | python3 -c "import sys,json;d=json.load(sys.stdin);p=[x for x in d['packages'] if x['name']=='$pkg'][0];print([t['src_path'] for t in p['targets'] if 'lib' in t['kind']][0])")
python3 "$(dirname "$0")/mark.py" "$(dirname "$root")" "$root"
cd "$(dirname "$root")/.."
export CARGO_TARGET_DIR=$out/target CC=/usr/lib/llvm-23/bin/clang CFLAGS="-fprofile-instr-generate -fcoverage-mapping"
export RUSTFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage" RUSTDOCFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage -Z unstable-options --persist-doctests $out/doctests"
cargo "+$nightly" test -p "$pkg" "$@" --target $host --no-run --message-format=json 2>"$out/build.err" \
  | python3 -c 'import sys,json
for l in sys.stdin:
  try: d=json.loads(l)
  except: continue
  if d.get("reason")=="compiler-artifact" and d.get("executable") and d["target"]["kind"]!=["custom-build"] and d.get("profile",{}).get("test"): print(d["target"]["name"],d["target"]["kind"][0],d["executable"])' > "$out/bins.txt"
cat "$out/bins.txt"; tail -2 "$out/build.err"
while read -r name kind exe; do
  suite=$([ "$kind" = lib ] && echo lib || echo "$name")
  mkdir -p "$out/prof/$suite"; echo "== $suite"
  LLVM_PROFILE_FILE="$out/prof/$suite/%p-%m.profraw" "$exe" > "$out/$suite.log" 2>&1 || echo "rc=$? in $suite"
  grep 'test result' "$out/$suite.log"
  "$exe" --list 2>/dev/null | grep -c ': test$' > "$out/$suite.count"
done < "$out/bins.txt"
mkdir -p "$out/prof/doc"; echo "== doc"

#!/bin/bash
# run.sh <repo> <package> <cov dir>: build a coverage-instrumented scratch copy of the safe
# crate against the `coverage` variant, its test items under #[coverage(off)], and run each
# suite alone into <cov dir>/prof/<suite>: lib, each integration test binary, and doc. Each
# binary links the variant's C statically, so its profiles count the C and the Rust alike.
# report.py then reads the figures (testing spec, Coverage), with the variant's static archive
# as the C object.
set -euo pipefail
repo=$1 pkg=$2 out=$3
host=x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
nightly=$(sed -n 's/^nightly = "\(.*\)"$/\1/p' "$repo/Cargo.toml")
tree=$out/tree
rm -rf "$out"; mkdir -p "$tree/crustify" "$out/prof"
(cd "$repo" && tar -cf - --exclude=./target --exclude=./crustify --exclude=./c --exclude=./.git .) | (cd "$tree" && tar -xf -)
ln -s "$repo/c" "$tree/c"
ln -s "$repo/crustify/artifacts" "$tree/crustify/artifacts"
ln -s "$repo/crustify/builds" "$tree/crustify/builds"
python3 "$(dirname "$0")/mark.py" "$tree/src" "$tree/src/lib.rs"
cd "$tree"
export CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=coverage CARGO_TARGET_DIR=$out/target
export RUSTFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage" RUSTDOCFLAGS="-C instrument-coverage -Z unstable-options --persist-doctests $out/doctests"
cargo "+$nightly" test -p "$pkg" --target $host --no-run --message-format=json 2>"$out/build.err" \
  | python3 -c 'import sys,json
for l in sys.stdin:
  try: d=json.loads(l)
  except: continue
  if d.get("reason")=="compiler-artifact" and d.get("executable") and d["target"]["kind"]!=["custom-build"] and d.get("profile",{}).get("test"): print(d["target"]["name"],d["target"]["kind"][0],d["executable"])' > "$out/bins.txt"
cat "$out/bins.txt"
while read -r name kind exe; do
  suite=$([ "$kind" = lib ] && echo lib || echo "$name")

  echo "== $suite"

The gates of testing-gates' Regressions section, run exactly so:

1. The tree's commit (`--rev`, HEAD by default), or its working tree with
   `--working-tree`, is copied to a snapshot, `<tree>/crustify/tmp/gates-<label>`, so that
   work goes on in the tree while the gates run. Each submodule, and each `--link` path
   (such as the variants' builds dir), is symlinked from the tree into it, and the snapshot
   is made a git repository, since a test may discover the repository it runs in.
2. Each skip of `--skip-file` is checked against its test binary's `--list` before any
   stage runs: a skip that names no test fails the run. A run with skips passes libtest
   `--exact`, so that a skip takes its one test and no other whose name holds it. A variant
   stage's skip must also name one test of the whole workspace, since that stage runs
   every binary with the same arguments: a name another binary holds too fails the run.
3. The stages run in the order given:
   - `lint`: the workspace's format check, `cargo +<nightly> fmt --all --check`, then its
     lints with warnings denied, `<runner> plain clippy --workspace --all-targets
     [--features <features>] -- -D warnings`, once with no feature and once for each
     `--lint-features`, such as the export features of the modules not yet switched;
   - a variant (`plain` and each sanitizer but `bsan`): the workspace's tests,
     `<runner> <variant> test --workspace --no-fail-fast`, with that stage's skips;
   - `miri`: the package's test binaries built once on the pinned nightly, then one
     `cargo miri test` per test binary, side by side, each skipping `compile_fail`;
   - `bsan`: the test binaries built once, then one invocation per test binary, side by
     side, each under `--timeout`, with that stage's skips.
4. Each run writes `<logs>/<stage>[-<binary>].log`, a lint run
   `<logs>/lint-fmt.log` and `<logs>/lint-clippy[-<features>].log`; `<logs>/summary.json` and
   `summary.txt` record each run's command, exit status, duration, test-result lines and
   failed tests. A run that exceeds its timeout reports `timed_out`.

The skip file holds one skip per line, `<stage> <binary> <exact test name>`, the binary
being `lib` or an integration test's name; `#` starts a comment.

The job count is the environment's: `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS` for builds, `RUST_TEST_THREADS` for
each binary's tests, as concurrency describes. The exit status is 0 when every run
passed, 1 when any failed, and 2 when the run could not start.

content.content:
# Goals

This file states what Crustify is for and how it evolves. Every change to Crustify is judged
against these goals, whether it changes its skills, its agents or its tools.

A rule that serves none of these goals is removed. Where two goals are in tension, they are
weighed for the case at hand, and the weighing is stated.

The goals evolve too, from the same evidence as everything else:

- a goal the campaigns keep missing;
- a goal no decision ever cites;
- two goals that keep conflicting the same way; or
- a well-founded change that none of the goals serves.

A change to the goals is proposed as Crustify's `evolution` skill describes. It lands only
with the user's approval.

Each goal names its *fitness*: what a campaign measures to tell how far the goal is met. Each
thing measured is a *measure*. A measure is read from one of two sources, and no run is made
only to take it:

- what the campaign's runs produce anyway: the dashboard, the review reports, the gates and
  the plan; or
- a rerun the campaign's reviews already make.

A *tier* is one of the checks that code meets one after another. An *escape* is a defect
caught by a later tier than the one that read the code first. Later tiers include:

- a module pass after a wave's review;
- a switch;
- a revisit; and
- a ship point's gates.

Worse work could improve some measures. Such a measure is *paired* with the measure that
catches the worse work, which is its *pair*, and neither is read alone. When there are more
escapes, fewer findings is no gain. When the work is redone, cheaper work is no gain.

Some measures are held by no artifact yet. Such a measure is marked **Not taken yet**. Until
it is taken, what it measures is judged, not measured.

Under each goal, **Measure** states a measure, **Paired with** names its pair, and **Not
taken yet** names what no artifact holds yet.

## 1. Safety

No undefined behaviour is reachable from safe Rust. The unsafe code that remains sits in its
regions, and is sound for every input.

### The unsafe surface

- **Measure.** What a deterministic scan counts on each landing:
  - raw pointers and `unsafe fn`s on the public API;
  - unsafe lines and raw dereferences; and
  - unsafe code outside its regions.

  The first two fall as a module goes from wrapped to ported and through its later stages.
  The third is zero throughout.
- **Paired with** soundness, below. Calling an unsound function safe takes an obligation off
  the API, and so lowers this measure.

### Soundness

- **Measure.** The defects a reproducer proves, as the review reports file them by kind.
  These defects are undefined behaviour and contracts that can be broken.
- **Paired with** the escapes among these defects.
- **Not taken yet.** The tier that caught a defect. Also the unsafe sites a review read,
  which the defects are counted against.

## 2. Equivalence

The Rust keeps the C's specified behaviour, not its bugs. The specified behaviour is what
the C's documentation, tests and consumers rely on.

- **Measure.**
  - The target's own tests passing over the Rust at each switch, against their recorded
    baseline.
  - The inputs and states on which the Rust is compared with the C it replaces, with no
    difference left unexplained.
  - The differences made on purpose, each documented and held by a test.
- **Paired with** the differences found after the comparison ended. They are found by a
  review, at a switch, or by a consumer.
- **Not taken yet.** The inputs compared and the deliberate differences, as figures. Each
  run's notes alone hold them.

## 3. Idiomatic Rust

The API a Rust consumer sees is native Rust: ownership, borrowing, errors, iteration and
traits. It is not C's conventions behind a Rust syntax.

- **Measure.** The C forms that Safety's scan still counts on the public API: raw and
  untyped pointers, and obligations handed to callers. Also the ergonomics and idiom
  findings that reviews file, counted per item reviewed.
- **Paired with** the ergonomics and idiom findings that a later tier or a consumer makes on
  an item an earlier review passed. A review that reads less finds less.
- **Not taken yet.** Which tier made a finding.

## 4. Performance

The emitted Rust costs no more than native Rust would. Where tokens and time buy
accuracy, the harness spends them.

### The harness

- **Measure.** Cost and wall time per translated item, reviews and switches included.
- **Paired with** what was redone: batches run again, gates rerun and merges made twice.
- **Paired with** Safety's and Equivalence's measures: cheaper work with more escapes is not
  cheaper.

### The emitted Rust

- **Measure.** The emitted Rust's time and memory against the C it replaces, on the target's
  own workloads.
- **Paired with** Safety's and Equivalence's measures, since a check dropped is time saved.
- **Not taken yet.** The whole measure.
  <!-- TODO: no campaign benchmarks what it ports; which workloads, and at which event,
  is not specified. -->

## 5. Verification

content.content:
### G2. Compiler-precise

A fact comes from the compiler's own resolution, never from source text: a
callee is identified by its definition, a type by its `DefId`, an ABI by the
signature's. A name is matched only where the compiler cannot say more, and
only against a caller's input or a fixed vocabulary.

*Checked by:* the driver reads names only in the tables
[`analysis.md`](analysis.md) lists.

### G8. General rules, no overfitting

A rule follows from Rust's and C's semantics and holds for every crate. It
matches no names, paths or conventions of one crate or one tool that builds
crates, and does not special-case the crate that motivated it. A convention's
vocabulary, such as ffibox's, is a fixed set of arms its flag turns on, read
from the convention's own declarations.

*Checked by:* each rule has a fixture written for it, and its effect is
measured on a crate other than the one that motivated it (G10).

## Validation

### G9. Every counter is tested

Each counter has a fixture whose expected count is derived by hand, item by
item, with the items that must NOT move it beside those that must. Every site a
counter records is checked to be addressable and to sum to the counter.

*Checked by:* the canary, cells and interop suites, and `SiteTests`.

### G10. Every change is measured on real code

A change to a counter is run on the crates under [`examples/`](../examples)
before it lands, and its commit states what moved and that nothing else did.
An unexplained difference is a defect until it is explained.

*Checked by:* the commit message, and the rescanned examples.

### G11. Readings are checked against the source

A new counter's sites are read on at least one real crate, to show that what it
counts is what its row says it counts.

*Checked by:* the commit message names the crate and what its sites showed.

## Interface
# The seam list names `from_raw` but not its inverse `into_raw`

Status: `landed`, as crustify `200bc65` on `devel`; scans name `into_raw` from the next wave, which the dashboard's Notes say.

## Signal

A tool's figures that the source contradicts: the `ffimap` skill's seam list, which every
scan passes as `--seams`, names ffibox's adoption `from_raw` and the run hand-offs
`from_raw_parts` / `into_raw_parts`, but not `into_raw`, the hand-off ffibox's own owners
give a single pointer (`CBox::into_raw`, `CStrBox::into_raw`, `CArc::into_raw`). An owner
that follows ffibox's naming then counts its give-up as pointer management a consumer faces,
while the adoption that reverses it is plumbing.

## Evidence

wave 184 batch 1 (`src/util/strlist.c` module pass), its scan with the skill's seams
(`crustify/tmp/ffimap-base-sites.json` in the batch's worktree): `raw_ptr.fn_sig_ret.safe.pub`
lists `src/libgit2/src/util/strlist.rs` lines 294, 302, 516 and 523. Three are seams
(`StrList::into_raw_parts`, `StrList::as_ptr`, `NullStrList::as_ptr`); line 516,
`NullStrList::into_raw`, the give-up of a NULL-terminated array, is not, though its inverse
`NullStrList::from_raw` is counted under `of_which.seam`. It is the crate's first `into_raw`
returning a pointer; the five others (`trailer.rs`, `buf.rs`, `index.rs`, `commit.rs`) return
C structs by value.

## Destination

The spec: `skills/tools/ffimap/SKILL.md`, the seam list of its preamble and its `--seams`
example (the binder's and translator's, as the tool skill's Binding section is; the
preamble is shared).

## Change

Add `into_raw` to the list ("the ownership hand-offs `from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`,
`into_raw`, `from_c`, `into_c` and `as_c_ptr`") and to the example's `--seams`. Two scans
compare only with the same seams, so the change takes effect from the next wave, and the
dashboard's Notes name the wave it starts in.

## Validation

None run: the seam share of one counter moves by one site in this crate today.

# An adopted spec, outcome or parser lends its borrows for any lifetime its adopter names

- **finding**: `contracts/ffi_import/adopted-handles-outlive-their-borrows`
- **batch**: `wave-186/batch-3/run-1`, the review of `wave-186/batch-0` (`8a149ac08`) and
  `wave-186/batch-2` (`fe6b85bfa`), `opt.h`'s types
- **items**: `st::cli_opt_spec`, `st::cli_opt`, `st::cli_opt_parser`
- **affected commit**: `fe6b85bfa`
- **where**: `src/git2/src/cli/opt.rs`, `mod ffi_import`: the handles `define_ctype!` mints
  for `Spec<'p>`, `Opt<'p>` and `Parser<'p>`, their public `unsafe` seams
  `CRefSeam::from_ptr` / `CMutSeam::from_ptr`, and the getters whose `SAFETY:` comments rest
  on "its handle's adoption": `SpecRef::{target, name, value_name, help}`,
  `OptRef::{spec, arg, value}`, `ParserRef::{specs, args}`, `ParserMut::args_mut` and
  `Arg::as_c_str`

## Finding

The three layouts carry `'p`, the lifetime of the strings, variables, spec table and
argument array they point at. Their getters lend those for `'p`, not for the handle's
borrow `'a`. For a handle built in Rust that is sound: each setter takes a `&'p` borrow.
For a handle adopted from a pointer, the getters' `SAFETY:` comments say "a spec C built
holds, by its handle's adoption, `NULL` or a string that lives unchanged for `'p`". No
contract asks an adopter for that. The only public adoption is ffibox's `CRefSeam::from_ptr`
and `CMutSeam::from_ptr`, whose `# Safety` is `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s: "`ptr` must address a
live, initialised `Self::C` (or be null) that outlives `'a`, and nothing may write it while
the handle lives except through a `Mut` derived from the same borrow". It says nothing of
`'p`, which the adopter picks freely, nor of the `value` pointer matching its `type`, which
`target()` casts by. A caller who honours that contract still gets dangling borrows from
safe getters.

## Evidence

The reproducer, `src/main.rs` beside this report, builds a spec in Rust storage whose name
is a short-lived `CString`. It adopts the spec through `SpecRef::<'_, 'static>::from_ptr`,
keeping every clause of the stated contract: the spec is live and initialised, it outlives
the handle, and nothing writes it. It reads `name()`, a `&'static CStr`, then drops the spec
and the string. On `fe6b85bfa` Miri stops at the use (`run-affected.log`):

```
error: Undefined Behavior: constructing invalid value of type &std::ffi::CStr: encountered a dangling reference (use-after-free)
  --> src/main.rs:27:22

# `set_settings_ptr` admits callbacks that set a reason which dies before the parser

- **finding**: `contracts/ffi_import/settings-ptr-admits-a-reason-that-dies-first`
- **batch**: `wave-194/batch-5/run-1`, the `type` review of `deps/llhttp/api.c`'s folded waves,
  over `wave-194/batch-0` (`1ead111ee`) and `wave-194/batch-2` (`97dea9da3`)
- **items**: `fld::llhttp__internal_s.settings` (`ParserMut::set_settings_ptr`),
  `fld::llhttp__internal_s.reason` (`ParserRef::reason`)
- **affected commit**: `1ead111ee`, unchanged through `2a51ccb3f`
- **files**: `src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/llhttp.rs`

## Finding

`ParserRef::reason` is safe and follows the parser's `reason` pointer whenever it is called,
for the handle's borrow. Its `// SAFETY:` comment rests on who may set that pointer: llhttp
(its literals), `set_reason` (a `&'static CStr`) and "a handle built over C's parser". It
leaves out the callbacks of a table stored by `ParserMut::set_settings_ptr`, which run on a
parser Rust owns. llhttp lets every callback set any string as the reason:
`llhttp_set_error_reason` is to be "called in user callbacks right before returning the
errno" (`c/deps/llhttp/llhttp.h:730`), and its body stores the pointer
(`c/deps/llhttp/api.c:213`). `set_settings_ptr`'s `# Safety` asks only for a table "that stays
live and unchanged, and whose callbacks are sound to call with this parser and its `data`,
for as long as the parser executes with it". A callback that sets a reason its context owns
honours that, and so does a caller that frees the context once the parser is done executing.
The safe `reason()` then reads freed memory.

`Callback::from_fn`'s contract (`wave-194/batch-1`, `2c69341c3`), which the `Settings` getters
and `ParserMut::set_settings` rest on, is silent on the reason too. A C function it accepts
may serve any parser, so a reason it sets must live as long as the program. No caller of
`from_fn` passes a C function yet, so nothing reaches this one.

## Evidence

The reproducer stores a `static` table whose `on_url`, written as C writes one, reads its
`Context` from the parser's `data` and calls `llhttp_set_error_reason` with the context's
`CString`, returning `HPE_USER`. It sets the table and the context through the two `unsafe`
setters, parses `GET /refused HTTP/1.1\r\n`, clears the table and `data`, and frees the
context, every step within the setters' contracts. Then the safe `parser.as_ref().reason()`
reads the freed string (`run-affected.log`, exit 134):

```text
=== crustify/reviews/modules/libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.c/wave-194/batch-6/contracts/ffi_export/gateway-handles-claim-more-than-c-keeps/report.md
# The gateway's handles claim of C's parsers more than C keeps

- **finding**: `contracts/ffi_export/gateway-handles-claim-more-than-c-keeps`
- **batch**: `wave-194/batch-6/run-1`, the `symbol` review of `deps/llhttp/api.c`'s folded
  waves
- **items**: api.c's exports under `ffi-export-deps-llhttp-api-c` (`fn::llhttp_execute`,
  `fn::llhttp_finish`, the 23 `fn::llhttp__on_<slot>` and the others built on `parser_mut`),
  and `ffi_import`'s `ParserMut::table`, which the dispatchers read
- **affected commit**: `b3d6b9b37` (`parser_mut` since `2a51ccb3f`)
- **files**: `src/libgit2/deps/llhttp/api.rs`

## Finding

Every export but `llhttp_get_error_pos` and `llhttp_get_error_reason` builds its parser's
exclusive handle with `parser_mut`, whose `// SAFETY:` comment vouches for the handle's
invariant on this ground:

> its `settings` and `data` meet `set_settings_ptr`'s and `set_data`'s contracts, which is
> what C's own callers of `llhttp_execute` promise

and `table()`'s comment counts "C's callers of api.c's functions with their own tables" among
those that meet `set_settings_ptr`'s contract "for as long as the parser holds it". Since
`b3d6b9b37`, those contracts ask that the table's callbacks be sound with the parser's `data`
*at any time* while the parser holds the table, since the dispatchers are safe methods. C's
callers promise no such thing. libgit2's HTTP client, the only C that calls these exports
with a table, installs a `static` table once (`reset_parser`, `llhttp_init`,
`c/src/libgit2/transports/httpclient.c:917-922`), points `data` at a stack
`http_parser_context` only around its own parses, and sets it NULL again before returning
(`httpclient.c:1271`/`1283`, `1458`/`1473`, `1503`/`1529`, `1548`/`1565`). Its callbacks
dereference `data` unconditionally (`on_header_complete`, `httpclient.c:161-165`, and the
others at `228`, `263`, `351`, `395`, `417`). Between those calls a dispatcher would follow
NULL.

The exports are nonetheless sound: each builds its handle for its own call, uses it for that
call's one operation and drops it before returning, and during the call C's caller keeps its
table and its context, as llhttp asks of it. So the invariant the comments claim does not
hold, but the one the code needs does. A justification resting on what C does not promise is
a contracts finding; no reproducer is needed, since nothing unsound is reachable.

## Fix

- **finding**: `ub_export/args-slot-handed-to-c-through-a-dead-borrow`
- **batch**: `wave-186/batch-7/run-1`, the module pass of `git2/src/cli/opt.c`.
- **item**: `fn::cli_opt_parse`, and `fn::cli_opt_parser_next` and `fn::cli_opt_foreach`: their
  exports in `src/git2/src/cli/opt.rs`'s `ffi_export` (`wave-186/batch-5`, `c62dee857`), over
  `take_bare` (`fn::parse_arg`), which stores an `Args` spec's position, and `Parser::into_args`.
- **affected commit**: `961150dd9`, the wave's tip; since `c62dee857`.
- **class**: undefined behaviour reached from C through an export, within `opt.h`'s contract, as
  Miri's default aliasing model, Stacked Borrows, defines it: the campaign's Miri gate.

## Finding

A `CLI_OPT_TYPE_ARGS` spec's variable is a `char **`, which C reads after the parse:
`cmd_hash_object.c` walks `filenames` to `argv`'s `NULL`. The C parse stores `&args[idx]`, its
caller's own pointer plus an index. The export adopted `argv + 1` as a `&mut [Arg]`, and
`take_bare` stored the position from a shared reborrow of it,
`ArgsSlot::set(parser.as_ref().args().get(idx..))`: a pointer that grants access only while no
later borrow of the array takes it away. Two do, before C reads it:

- `parse` itself, which hands its array back through `Parser::into_args`, a
  `slice::from_raw_parts_mut` over it: a unique reborrow, which invalidates the stored pointer
  before `cli_opt_parse` returns; and
- any later export over the same `argv`, whose adoption is a unique reborrow of the array:
  `cmd_hash_object.c -w` opens the repository, and `common.c`'s `parse_common_options` parses
  `argv + 1` again through `cli_opt_foreach`, before the files are walked.

C then reads `argv` through a pointer whose access Rust ended. Under Tree Borrows the same run is
accepted, since neither reborrow writes the array here; Stacked Borrows, Miri's default and the
model of the campaign's Miri gate, reports it. Once the module switches, the gateway's tests run

# The lent atomic's justification says every racing access is atomic, which C's plain reads contradict

- **finding**: `contracts/ffi_import/lent-atomic-justification-omits-plain-c-reads`
- **batch**: `wave-226/batch-4/run-1`, the review of `wave-226/batch-0` (`3f7f3ab89`),
  `src/util/thread.c`'s types
- **items**: `fld::git_atomic32.val` and `fld::git_atomic64.val` (`Atomic32Ref::val`,
  `Atomic64Ref::val`)
- **affected commit**: `3f7f3ab89`
- **where**: `src/libgit2/src/util/thread.rs`, `mod ffi_import`, `atomic_type!`'s `val`: its
  second `// SAFETY:` comment and its doc comment
- **class**: `nit`
- **evidence**: reading: the C sources cited below; no reproducer, since the justification is
  imprecise and no input breaks what the code relies on
- **conditions**: any; `GIT_THREADS` with `GIT_BUILTIN_ATOMIC`, this build's
- **pattern**: `aliasing-at-the-boundary`
- **tiers**: caught by this review batch; `wave-226/batch-0`'s own gates had it in scope and
  passed it, as no gate can catch a comment

## Finding

`val` lends the field as `&'a AtomicI32` (or `AtomicI64`) through `from_ptr`, whose
contract forbids mixing conflicting atomic and non-atomic accesses without synchronisation.
Its `// SAFETY:` comment rests on this:

> Every access it may race with is atomic: the handle's other holders reach the value only
> through this, and C writes it only through `thread.h`'s atomic operations (the module
> documentation), of the same size.

and its doc comment says C "reads and writes it with sequentially consistent operations
(`SeqCst`) alone". C's writes are all atomic, but its reads are not. It reads some shared
values plainly:

- `t->cancelled.val` in `c/src/libgit2/transports/smart.c:42` and
  `smart_protocol.c:492`, `571`, `631`, `701`, `725` and `733`. `git_smart__cancel` sets the
  flag with `git_atomic32_set`, from whichever thread calls `git_remote_stop`.
- `git_cache__current_storage.val` in `c/src/libgit2/settings.c:181`, beside
  `cache_store`'s and `cache_free`'s `git_atomic_ssize_add` on other threads.

The module documentation says so, and says the race is C's own. The comment the code rests
on, and the accessor's own documentation, say the opposite. That comment is what the port
batches of `git_atomic32_set` and its siblings build on: their exports adopt C's
`git_atomic32 *` and write through `val`, so a reader judging an export from the comment
would take a race that exists for granted as absent.

What the code relies on still holds. Every access Rust makes is atomic, and so is every write
C makes. A plain C read races with a concurrent write whoever makes it, Rust through `val`
or C through its own `__atomic_store_n`. That is a race of the C, which the binding neither
adds nor can remove. So the finding is an imprecise justification, a `nit`, and not a
contract that can be broken.

## Fix

In this batch's second commit, the comment says what holds. Every write `val` may race with
is atomic and of the same size, and so is every Rust read. C's plain reads of a shared value
(the module documentation) race with any write made on another thread, C's own atomic ones
as much as one made through `val`: a race of the C's, which lending the atomic neither adds
nor can remove. The doc comment says C writes the integer with sequentially consistent
operations alone, and reads it with them but for the plain reads the module documentation
names. The code does not change.

# The atomics and the thread lack `Debug`, and the atomics `From` their integer

- **finding**: `ergonomics/atomics-and-thread-lack-standard-traits`
- **batch**: `wave-226/batch-4/run-1`, the review of `wave-226/batch-0` (`3f7f3ab89`),
  `src/util/thread.c`'s types
- **items**: `st::git_atomic32` (`Atomic32`, `Atomic32Ref`, `Atomic32Mut`), `st::git_atomic64`
  (`Atomic64`, `Atomic64Ref`, `Atomic64Mut`, and `AtomicSsize`, `tdf::git_atomic_ssize`),
  `st::git_thread` (`Thread`, `ThreadRef`, `ThreadMut`)
- **affected commit**: `3f7f3ab89`
- **where**: `src/libgit2/src/util/thread.rs`, `mod ffi_import`
- **class**: `nit`
- **evidence**: reading; `format!("{:?}", Atomic32::new(1))` does not compile on `3f7f3ab89`
  (E0277, `Atomic32` doesn't implement `Debug`)
- **conditions**: any
- **tiers**: caught by this review batch; `wave-226/batch-0`'s own gates had it in scope and
  passed it

## Finding

`reviewing`'s `ergonomics` objective names the standard traits a type lacks. The wrap is the
first batch to give these types a safe API, which their `port/layout` stages keep (waves 1445,
1620 and 2308), so their traits are reviewed here.

- None of the nine types implements `Debug`. `AtomicI32` and `AtomicI64`, which the atomics
  lend and stand in for, print their integer. The types this module's other batches add do
  implement it, as do the crate's other layout types and handles, and earlier reviews filed
  its absence on a handle (`legacy-wave-37/batch-0`'s `misc/entry-handles-lack-debug`). A
  ported struct that embeds a reference count, as every `git_refcount` holder will once its
  `port/layout` makes it native, cannot `#[derive(Debug)]` while `Atomic32` lacks it.
- `Atomic32` and `Atomic64` have no `From<i32>` / `From<i64>`, which `AtomicI32` and
  `AtomicI64` have, so `let count: Atomic32 = 1.into()` does not compile where
  `let count: AtomicI32 = 1.into()` does.

## Fix

In this batch's second commit, in `ffi_import`, as safe impls beside the handles:

- `atomic_type!` gives each shared handle a `Debug` that prints the integer through the
  standard atomic's own `Debug` (`fmt::Debug::fmt(self.val(), f)`), so that it prints as
  `AtomicI32` does. The value and the exclusive handle print as their shared handle. It also
  gives each value `From` its integer, as `new` builds it.
- `ThreadRef` prints `Thread { thread: <id> }` through its getter, and `Thread` and
  `ThreadMut` print as it.

Each reads only what the safe getters read, and the change adds no unsafe code. Nothing is
removed or changed, so the port batches of the module's symbols that build on these types
keep compiling.

## Tests

`tests/unit_pub/src/util/thread.rs`:
`atomics_print_and_convert_as_the_standard_atomics_do` prints a value, each handle and an
`AtomicSsize`, compares them with `AtomicI32`'s output, and builds values with `From` and
`into`. `a_thread_prints_its_id` prints a zeroed thread and its handles. Both pass plain and
under Miri.

  `AtomicI64` have, so `let count: Atomic32 = 1.into()` does not compile where
  `let count: AtomicI32 = 1.into()` does.

In this batch's second commit, in `ffi_import`, as safe impls beside the handles:

- `atomic_type!` gives each shared handle a `Debug` that prints the integer through the
  standard atomic's own `Debug` (`fmt::Debug::fmt(self.val(), f)`), so that it prints as
  `AtomicI32` does. The value and the exclusive handle print as their shared handle. It also
  gives each value `From` its integer, as `new` builds it.
- `ThreadRef` prints `Thread { thread: <id> }` through its getter, and `Thread` and
  `ThreadMut` print as it.

Each reads only what the safe getters read, and the change adds no unsafe code. Nothing is
removed or changed, so the port batches of the module's symbols that build on these types
keep compiling.

`tests/unit_pub/src/util/thread.rs`:
`atomics_print_and_convert_as_the_standard_atomics_do` prints a value, each handle and an
`AtomicSsize`, compares them with `AtomicI32`'s output, and builds values with `From` and
`into`. `a_thread_prints_its_id` prints a zeroed thread and its handles. Both pass plain and
under Miri.

# Layout types whose state is written through shared access

Status: `open`.

## Signal

One representation written by hand (`evolution` §2), and a rule that forces a hand-written
layer `define_ctype!` could cover. `define_ctype!` lays a type out as its C struct alone,
`#[repr(transparent)] struct Foo(ffi::foo, PhantomData<…>)`. A value Rust holds hands out
its handles from `&self`, so they carry a pointer that may only be read through, as
`CRefSeam::as_ptr`'s documentation says. That is right for every C type whose writes go
through an exclusive handle. It is wrong for one whose state its holders change through
shared access, as an atomic counter's is: no write through a shared handle is sound over
a value Rust holds, and a `static` of such a type may be placed in read-only memory.

## Evidence

- `wave-226/batch-0/run-1`, `src/util/thread.c`, wraps `git_atomic32` and `git_atomic64`
  (`thread.h`): one `volatile int` or `int64_t` that libgit2's threads change only with
  `__atomic` builtins. Examples are every `git_refcount`, the runtime's `init_count`, and
  the object cache's `git_cache__current_storage`. The port batches that follow port
  `git_atomic32_inc` and its siblings over them, and the runtime's globals become Rust
  `static`s. Every write to these types goes through shared access.
- With `define_ctype!`, `Atomic32::new(0).as_ref().val().fetch_add(1, SeqCst)`, through
  `AtomicI32::from_ptr` on the projected field, is a write through a pointer derived from a
  shared borrow of a type with no `UnsafeCell`. That write is UB. `reproducer/`, beside this
  proposal, does it over ffibox `568bcb5`, and `cargo +nightly-2026-10-08 miri run` stops it:
  "Undefined Behavior: … only grants SharedReadOnly permission", the tag created by
  `define_ctype!`'s `as_ref`. So
  the run hand-wrote both layout types over `UnsafeCell<ffi::git_atomic32>`. It wrote one
  local `macro_rules!`, `atomic_type!` in `src/libgit2/src/util/thread.rs`, of about 140
  lines, which restates `define_ctype!`'s expansion: the layout type, both handles over
  `CBorrowedPtr`, `unsafe impl CCell`, the seams, and `as_ref` / `as_mut`. The only change
  is the `UnsafeCell`.
- `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s contract (ffibox `568bcb5`) lets nothing write the object while a
  shared handle lives, except through a `Mut` of the same borrow, or under a lock that
  every read through `Ref` takes. An atomic takes no lock. Each of its reads is atomic,
  and so is each concurrent write C makes. So the port's export of `git_atomic32_inc`
  adopts `a` as an `Atomic32Ref` while other C threads increment the same count. That keeps
  the atomics' own soundness argument, but not the trait's literal text. The record's row
  for `ffibox-ref-contract-self-locking` widened that text for a self-locking object; an
  object of atomics is the lock-free case of the same rule.
- G9's handle rule is "no Rust reference over foreign memory that anything may write
  while the reference lives". Read literally, it forbids the `&'a AtomicI32` the run's
  `val` accessor lends. The hazard G9 excludes is a reference that asserts what is false:
  immutability, or exclusive access. A shared reference to a standard atomic asserts
  neither. It asserts liveness, alignment, and that every concurrent access is atomic,
  which is the atomic's contract. The standard library offers `AtomicI32::from_ptr` for
  exactly this interoperation.

## Goal

Crustify's Safety goal (soundness), and ffibox's G1 (mirror standard Rust: a C atomic
field's safe form is the standard atomic) and G12 (obligations local: the contract an
atomics wrapper relies on is stated by the trait it implements, not argued against it).
The fitness measure: the hand-written `unsafe impl CCell` count in the campaign's crate,
which this run raised by two. No `ub` or `contracts` finding should appear on a layout
type written through shared access.

## Destination

ffibox: `define_ctype!` (`src/macros.rs`), `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s and `CRefSeam::as_ptr`'s
contracts (`src/traits.rs`), `docs/borrows.md`'s conventions, `docs/hand-written.md`'s
scope, and G9's handle row in `docs/goals.md`. Once that lands, `binding-types`' Field accessors
section gains the case's line: a field C changes through shared access, with atomic
operations alone, is lent by the shared handle as the standard atomic of its width, and its
layout type is declared `interior`.

## Change

1. `define_ctype!` takes an option, `interior`, for a C type whose state its holders write
   through shared access. It lays the type out as
   `#[repr(transparent)] struct Foo(UnsafeCell<ffi::foo>, PhantomData<…>)`. Its `as_ref`
   then hands out a pointer that may be written through, as `UnsafeCell::get`'s does, and a
   `static` of it is writable. All else is unchanged: `CCell`, the handles and the seams.
   The layout type stays `!Sync` until the binding asserts `Sync`.
2. `CCell::ref_from_ptr`'s contract admits a third kind of concurrent write. Beside writes
   through a `Mut` of the same borrow, and writes under a lock every read through `Ref`
   takes, it admits writes made atomically to bytes that every access through `Ref` makes
   atomically, of the same size. `CRefSeam::as_ptr`'s note extends to such a type: one
   declared `interior` may be written through `as_ptr` atomically, even when Rust holds
   the value.
3. G9's handle row and `docs/borrows.md`'s "No reference covers C memory anything may
   write" exempt a shared reference to a standard atomic over a field that only atomic
   accesses reach. Such a reference asserts no immutability and no exclusive access.

## Validation

Not made: this proposal is the binder's, and ffibox is outside its evolution scope. The
run's `atomic_type!` is the expansion that `interior` would emit. Its tests are evidence
for that expansion:

- `tests/unit_pub/src/util/thread.rs`, `tests/ub_safe/src/util/thread.rs` and
  `tests/ub_unsafe/src/util/thread.rs`;
- a `static` written from four threads; and
- shared handles and a lent `&AtomicI32` incremented from four threads at once.

They are clean under Miri and TSan. A change would add these as ffibox tests, with a
`compile_fail` case that a non-`interior` type still hands out a read-only pointer.

## Row

| change | from | landed as | signal | recurrence signal | status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `define_ctype!` takes `interior`, a layout over `UnsafeCell` for state written through shared access; `ref_from_ptr` admits atomic writes to bytes every `Ref` access reaches atomically; G9 exempts a reference to a standard atomic | `libgit2-crustify`, `ffibox-atomic-layout-types` | — | `git_atomic32` / `git_atomic64` were laid out by hand over `UnsafeCell`, since `define_ctype!`'s values hand out read-only pointers, and the adoption the atomics' port makes broke `ref_from_ptr`'s text | a hand-written `CCell` over `UnsafeCell`, or a `ub` finding of a write through a shared handle of a value Rust holds | — |

## Review

None yet.

"""report.py <cov dir> <name>=<dir>[:<dir>...][@<compilation dir>],... --c <C object>...
Merges each suite's profiles under <cov dir>/prof/, the four suites' union as TOTAL and every
suite's as ALL, and prints the TOTAL line of `llvm-cov report` for each named scope, with the C
objects and every test and doctest binary as objects for every suite. A scope's @<dir>
resolves the relative paths a C build recorded. MERGED=1 reuses the merged profiles, and ONLY=<suite> reports that one alone.
A scope written `<name>=@c`, such as `C=@c`, reads the C objects alone, with no source filter:
the archive holds only the link unit's TUs, whatever paths their build recorded. Any other
scope fails when a file it reports lies outside its dirs: llvm-cov falls back to every object
when its filters match no source, which would count the test binaries' std and Rust as C.
The C objects are those of the coverage variant's static archive, its `static` in build.json
(crustify/builds/coverage/crustify/libcrustify.a), which the test binaries link: each binary holds
only the TUs it reaches, so the archive, which llvm-cov reads member by member, gives every TU
its place in the denominator, one no test reaches at zero."""
out0=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1])
nightly=os.environ.get("NIGHTLY") or next(l.split('"')[1] for l in open(out0/"tree"/"Cargo.toml") if l.startswith("nightly = "))
sysroot=subprocess.run(['rustc','+'+nightly,'--print','sysroot'],capture_output=True,text=True,check=True).stdout.strip()
B=sysroot+'/lib/rustlib/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/bin/'
out=pathlib.Path(sys.argv[1]); scopes=dict(s.split('=',1) for s in sys.argv[2].split(','))
cobjs=sys.argv[sys.argv.index('--c')+1:]
bins=[l.split()[2] for l in (out/'bins.txt').read_text().splitlines()]
docs=[p for p in glob.glob(str(out/'doctests'/'**'/'rust_out'),recursive=True)]
objs=cobjs+bins+docs
suites=sorted(p.name for p in (out/'prof').iterdir() if any(p.glob('*.profraw')))
def merge(name,dirs):
    raws=[str(r) for d in dirs for r in (out/'prof'/d).glob('*.profraw')]
    prof=out/f'{name}.profdata'
    subprocess.run([B+'llvm-profdata','merge','-sparse','-o',str(prof)]+raws,check=True)
    return prof
def total(prof,srcs):
    cd=[]
    if srcs==['@c']: use,srcs=cobjs,[]
    else:
        use=objs
        if '@' in srcs[-1]: srcs[-1],c=srcs[-1].split('@'); cd=['-compilation-dir='+c]
    args=[B+'llvm-cov','report','-instr-profile',str(prof)]+cd+[use[0]]+sum((['-object',o] for o in use[1:]),[])+srcs
    r=subprocess.run(args,capture_output=True,text=True)
    if r.returncode: sys.exit(r.stderr[-2000:])
    lines=r.stdout.splitlines()
    if srcs and not cd:
        roots=[str(pathlib.Path(d).resolve()) for d in srcs]
        rows=[l.split()[0] for l in lines[2:] if l.strip() and not l.startswith(('-','TOTAL','Filename'))]
        stray=[f for f in rows if not any(str(pathlib.Path(f).resolve()).startswith(r+'/') or str(pathlib.Path(f).resolve())==r for r in roots)]
        if stray: sys.exit(f'scope {srcs} reports {len(stray)} files outside it, such as {stray[0]}: its filters match no source')
    t=[l for l in lines if l.startswith('TOTAL')][-1].split()
    # TOTAL regions missed cover functions missed exec lines missed cover branches missed cover
    return dict(lines=(int(t[7])-int(t[8]),int(t[7]),t[9]),functions=(int(t[4])-int(t[5]),int(t[4]),t[6]),regions=(int(t[1])-int(t[2]),int(t[1]),t[3]))
res={}
skip=os.environ.get('MERGED')
four=[x for x in suites if x!='doc']
only=os.environ.get('ONLY')

`bindings.rs`, which `+LoC` leaves out). Tests: 10 `unit_pub`, 5 `ub_safe` (shared and lent
atomics, a `static` and a compare-and-swap loop from four threads, an exclusive handle sent to a
thread), 4 `ub_unsafe` (`set_thread` within its contract: live threads' ids still owned by their
`JoinHandle`s, ids naming no thread, replacement, an array of objects), 5 compile-fail cases
(`thread_handles_not_send` split under `toolchain/`, since its notes quote `core`'s
`PhantomData`), and 4 doctests, 2 of them compile-fail. No test calls C, so no equivalence test
was written. The C over these layouts is the port batches' functions, and bindgen's layout
assertions and the module's `const` assertions compare the layouts. The 19 tests pass plain,
under ASan+UBSan and TSan, under Miri (the doctests too) and under BSan, each alone. The module's
and its 38 dependents' tests pass plain and under ASan+UBSan, 1,395 of them. The package (703
files) builds alone in bundled mode, as `package-gate-procedure` has it, with the workspace's Git
patch of ffibox. Its `lib` tests were not run, since the module has none.

Coverage: `run.sh` on this tree over gen5, read with `report.py` from the scratch tree's
`src/libgit2` (`C=@c` over `libcrustify.a`, Rust over the scratch `src/`). The unit column merges
`lib` and `unit_pub`. The tests reach no C, and the change adds only `thread.rs`'s instrumented
lines, so the base's figures are this run's less that file's. The pp cells are taken against
them: C `+0.00` in every suite, and Rust by the file's 34 lines, covered 20, 11, 0 and 30 by the
four suites. The base so derived reads `30.38`% / `77.32`% (`ub_safe`), `20.10`% / `17.64`%,
`43.75`% / `68.60`%, `34.38`% / `88.24`% and `47.46`% / `98.21`% (total). The Coverage stats
counts are the binaries' own test lists (unit: `lib` 908, `unit_pub` 251), where the table held
earlier counts. Worklist: `thread.rs` 34 of 34 lines, 10 of 10 functions and 36 of 36 regions. It
holds no branch, and its types have no states beyond their values, which the tests reach. The
safety audit scans (ffimap `50a800e`, `--sys-crates crate::sys,pcre2_sys`, no export feature)
are of the base `6faca73b7` and this tree. The Overview's Rust LoC moves by `code.loc.total`
(`+59`) and `code.tests.loc.total` (`+258`). `ffimap api` over the worklist (nightly `2026-10-08`,
ffibox's private rustdoc JSON) finds the 7 items `new`, `sys::libgit2` extended by `pthread_t`,
and every other module `kept`. `wrapped types` counts the three against the recorded `116`, and
its share is computed from the count, since the recorded `43.80`% was `113`'s. Usage cells are
the assistant's.

# API stability per C item

`ffimap api` measures a promise a C-to-Rust migration makes to its Rust
consumers: once a C item has a safe Rust API, wrapping it, porting it and its
later stages leave that API alone. It reads the crate's rustdoc JSON, finds the
Rust items that stand in for each C item through their anchors, and records
their consumer-facing surface twice: raw, as the signatures stand, and as the
**contract** a consumer may rely on whatever form a handle or an owner takes.
Two such records, one at the item's first landing and one after a later
landing, say whether the contract was kept, extended or changed. This document is what the two documents hold and every
rule behind them. The scan's counters are [`schema.md`](schema.md)'s and have
nothing to do with it.

## 1. Input

```sh
cargo +nightly-2026-10-07 rustdoc -p CRATE --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json
(cd ffibox && cargo +nightly-2026-10-07 rustdoc --lib -- -Z unstable-options \
    --output-format json --document-private-items)
ffimap api extract target/doc/CRATE.json --dep ffibox/target/doc/ffibox.json > before.json
```

`--dep` gives the rustdoc JSON of a crate the measured one depends on, and is
repeatable. The contracts of handles and owners that are aliases into ffibox
(`CBox`, `CArc`, `CVal`, …) need ffibox's, since the reborrows and trait impls
those forms inherit live there; it is made with `--document-private-items`
because the bounds rustdoc synthesises for ffibox's auto-trait impls name its
private fields' types. Without it those contracts are unresolved, as section 6
describes. The measure is pure Python over the JSON. It does not use the driver, so the
crate need not build on the driver's nightly, only document on one whose JSON
format it reads.

Rustdoc's JSON is unstable: each nightly writes a `format_version`, and the
shape moves with it. `ffimap api` reads **format 61**, which
nightly-2026-10-07 (the driver's pin) and nightly-2026-10-08 emit, and refuses
any other with an error naming the version it found. Support for a new format
is added by checking the fields `src/ffimap/rustdoc.py` reads against it and
adding it to `FORMAT_VERSIONS`.

## 2. C items and their stand-ins

A C item is keyed by its anchor's `<kind>::<path>`: `fn::git_mailmap_new`,
`st::git_mailmap`, `fld::git_buf.ptr`. An anchor is a doc-comment line of its
own, exactly ``Wraps `<kind>::<path>` `` or ``Replaces `<kind>::<path>` ``,
where the path is names separated by dots and a `fld` path names a member. Every
public item of the crate that carries one is a **stand-in** of that C item, and
an item carrying several (the accessor of two members) is a stand-in of each.

What the extract reports about the anchors themselves, under `anchors`:

- `malformed`: a line that tries to be an anchor and is not one -- the verb and
  a `kind::` path inside a sentence, with a trailing period, without backticks,
  or with a path that is not names. It keys nothing.
- `unknown_kinds`: anchors whose kind is not one of the convention's (`fn`,
  `st`, `un`, `enm`, `fnp`, `tdf`, `fld`, `glb`, `mac`), counted by kind. They
  are keyed as written.
- `without_alias`: anchors on an item with no `#[doc(alias)]` naming the
  anchor's path. An item whose own name is the anchor's path is left out:
  rustdoc rejects an alias equal to its item's name, and the name already
  answers a search for it.

## 3. Locators and paths

Each stand-in is named by a **locator**, which is how one landing's record is
matched with the next's:

| item | locator |
|---|---|
| a free item | its canonical path |
| an item of an inherent impl | `Ty::name` |
| an item of a trait impl | `<Ty as Trait<Args>>::name` |
| a trait's item, a variant, a field | its owner's locator `::name` |

Lifetime names in a locator are erased to `'_`.

A **canonical path** is the path a consumer names an item by. For an item of
the crate it is the path rustdoc's `paths` table gives its definition when that
path is public, else the shortest public path it is re-exported at, the first
in order among equals. An item defined in a private module and re-exported from
its parent is named by the parent's path, and a port that moves the definition
